speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This motion is acceptable, subject to the usual reservations concerning consent of the provincial governments.

Mr. Speaker, I am rising on a point of order. A practice seems to be growing up of ministers getting up and saying that these motions are being passed subject to the usual reservations, and the consequence is that the motions pass and in too many cases nothing whatever happens. It seems to me, sir, it would be much preferable if these motions were held up until consent had been secured beforehand. No one has ever objected to having a motion stand for a reasonable time for that purpose, and I should like to object to this motion passing with this qualification.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You would not wait the other day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is entirely wrong in saying that this is a practice that is growing up. This practice took very firm root in the time of the former government. As a matter of fact it goes back to the time of the late Mr. Mackenzie King. I well recall Mr. King taking the position quite firmly in the house with respect to such motions, that they should not pass unless there was a reservation making all iwance for the necessity of obtaining the consmt of the provincial government, if one were c mcerned, or, when it was something affecting external affairs, the consent of the government of the other country concerned. He stated the reason very clearly, namely that there could not be frank exchanges between governments unless there were some such reservation concerning the tabling of correspondence. So in proposing such reservations on the adoption of motions of this kind the ministers of the present government are simply following a practice that has been long established and was firmly recognized before we ever came into office.
The hon. gentleman raises a second point. He says it would be better practice if these motions were allowed to stand until the consent of the government concerned had been obtained. With great respect, Mr. Speaker, I submit that would be a wrong

Motions for Papers
practice. There should not be any direction given to ministers to seek the consent of some other government to the tabling of correspondence between them and ministers of the crown in right of the dominion until the house has passed the motion and decided that such correspondence ought to be produced if the other government is content to have it produced. Otherwise we would simply be putting the cart before the horse. Therefore I say that the present practice is firmly established and is the correct practice.

If I may say a word about both points raised by the Minister of Finance, I do not contest that when we were in office it was quite frequently said that the consent of the provincial government would have to be obtained. The phrase that is now being used is somewhat different, but I am not quarrelling about that. I thought the practice was a bad practice when we were in office, and I think it is a bad practice still.
What I do want to contest is the practice of having the house make a conditional kind of order which there is then no way whatever of having controlled. It does seem to me that the proper practice, and that provided in the rules, is that the government should either agree to the motion or oppose it. If the government is not prepared to agree to a motion until the consent of a provincial government is obtained, it would be preferable in order to maintain the rights of the opposition and private members generally, for the government to find out from the other government in advance whether or not this would be agreeable. If it would not be agreeable then, of course, they could oppose the motion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
May I say one
further word. The hon. gentleman says that nothing happens if these motions are passed subject to these reservations. With respect, Mr. Speaker, he is quite wrong. In these cases what the government does is communicate with the other government that was a party to the correspondence and ask the permission of that government for the tabling of the correspondence. Usually permission is forthcoming. Sometimes a minister of the other government will say that such and such a letter was personal and is not to be included, but it is a great mistake to say that nothing happens. The government, because of this reservation, seeks to comply with the conditions.
The other point is this. If the hon. gentleman seeks to render unnecessary a discussion of this kind, may I say that the way to meet that desire, if it is a desirable objective, is to provide in the terms of the motion itself for the production of the correspond-

ence with some other government that the correspondence be produced if the other government agrees.

May I just say a word on the point of order? With great respect to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, I think he is wrong in his premise today, namely that if the motion for the production of papers were allowed to stand it would not be a method of stalling the motion, but rather that the stalling could be brought about mainly by passing this motion. So far as I am concerned, and this motion happens to be in my name, I think the motion is in a much stronger position if it is passed by the house and the government is under instruction to produce this correspondence, subject to the usual reservation.
I have had experience, Mr. Speaker, with the other way of doing things. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources has taken the attitude that until certain agreements can be completed the information sought by this motion should not be produced. We had the standing procedure on that motion, and that was a stalling procedure. I think the best method is for the house to deal as expeditiously as possible with the motions when they are initially moved.
I should like to say a word on the point.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think I have heard enough to enable me to deal with the matter unless the hon. member has another approach, in which case I shall be glad to hear him.

Yes, I have. (Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I merely wish to say that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) seems deliberately to overlook that the Conservative government got into power by promising the people of Canada to restore the glory of parliament.
(Text):

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The point of order did not concern the practice of governments but the practice of the house. I think there is some difficulty raised by this point of order, because in effect what is being asked by the minister who suggests the limitation is that this motion be amended before it is put. I believe this can be done, with the consent of the mover, without any difficulty. This is what we have been doing. I understand that the mover of this motion is quite agreeable to the reservation being incorporated in the motion before it is put to the house; is that correct?
Yes.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
In order to overcome in the future in so far as the general practice is concerned, the technical difficulty which has

been raised by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, I see no solution other than to deal with each motion as it comes along, unless the house is willing to make an order that in all cases where provincial governments or other public bodies whose consent would be appropriate as a condition to the order being passed, such a reservation be considered a part of the motion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I much prefer the question of the Leader of the Opposition, because it does not introduce a lot of misnomers and empty Liberal shibboleths.
May I say that I have not seen the newspaper report from which the Leader of the Opposition purported to be quoting, but I may say that this question was raised whether the application of a monetary policy in the maritime area different from that applied in the rest of Canada was possible, and I pointed out that monetary policy has been confided by the parliament of Canada not to the government but to the Bank of Canada. That is clearly set forth in the statute law of this country.
However, as to the possibility of introducing, either through the Bank of Canada or by statutory enactment, a monetary policy for some particular region of the country different from that prevailing in the rest of Canada, I pointed out that such a thing would be quite impracticable in a country like this

because we have one central bank for the whole country. We have one currency for the country, and the issuance of all the currency is under one control. Our chartered banking system is national, and for these reasons a separate monetary policy for a section of the country would be quite impracticable.
However, the conversation did give me an opportunity to point out that special fiscal policies for a particular part of the country are quite possible, and this government has done more by means of fiscal measures to assist the Atlantic area of this country than any previous government has ever done.

Mr. Chairman, we are discussing a petition for divorce and we find, as in many of these cases, that the evidence presented to support the petition has been gathered by private investigators. The private investigators in this particular case have been before us on a number of previous occasions. I would suggest that they did not do enough investigating to prove that adultery had been committed and therefore that the divorce should be granted at this time.
In this particular case, Mr. Chairman, we find that very little consideration has been given to the support of the children. The indication is that the husband now makes a contribution of $15 a week. The wife, who has the two children with her, pays for their clothing, education and other considerations.

Private Bills-Divorce
I suggest that $15 is not sufficient to maintain two young girls and pay tor their education and raise them.
Mr. Chairman, this is one of the problems in these particular divorces. Here we are granting a divorce without being able to decide what is going to happen to the children and what maintenance is to be provided for the wife. This is a problem that concerns us very greatly. With respect to a married couple, obviously the maintenance of one of the partners in a marriage is implicit in the marriage; and when we dissolve the marriage, by our action we take away from one of the partners the right of maintenance that the individual has been used to.
The Senate committee which heard the evidence in this case consisted of 13 senators. The senators asked the usual questions. I think there was more questioning in this particular case by the senators than in some of the other cases. Senator Burchill made inquiries about the children. He asked first where the children were; who was living with them. He was interested in the family maintenance. In this case I would suggest that the answers he got, Mr. Chairman, would indicate that the children are not being looked after satisfactorily. If we granted this divorce without amendment, then there would be no maintenance for the children. I am interested in the children of this particular marriage. Senator Cameron asked some questions. First of all the chairman asked these questions:
Q. But you were not able to hold the family together?
A. No. Well at first they lived with my sister in law, the same one who takes care of mine. They all lived there.
By Senator Cameron:
Q. She looked after seven?
A. Yes.
Q. Did she not have any of her own?
A. No. But she is mentally and physically paralysed so she was very happy to be able to take care of my children.
I do not know why the senator left the questioning there, but it seems rather surprising to me that seven children would be left with a woman who was mentally and physically paralysed. It must make us wonder whether she was capable of looking after these children. I am surprised at this type of questioning, where the questions are asked only to establish this shocking situation and no further consideration is given to the matter of the maintenance of the children. I am sure this is sufficient to warrant the House of Commons, in its deliberations, in turning down the request for divorce.
It has been suggested, Mr. Chairman, that we have not the right to decide maintenance in these cases; that these matters should be referred to the courts in the province of

Quebec so that maintenance can be decided on, and then some further consideration be given to this particular case.
I see you shaking your head, Mr. Chairman. I presume you mean that is not possible. I am in agreement that it may not be possible; therefore I suggest that this divorce should not be granted at the present time. If it is granted, it would appear from the evidence that the children are going to be left to the care of another lady. The wife has to go to work, and she has not been able to earn enough money to keep them together. The $15 her husband pays her is not enough to keep the children together, so she has to go to work and leave the children in the care of a lady who, through no fault of her own, is neither mentally nor physically capable of looking after them. In this case Senator Burchill asked the following questions:
Q. When did you break up? Did he leave you or did you leave him?
A. He left me, just after the second child was born.
Q. He left you and went to another place to live?
A. I don't know where he went.
Q. Did he walk out of the house, or tell you where he was going?
A. He just didn't come back, and I thought he was going for the night, and as usual to gamble, but when I saw he didn't come back, what could X do? I had no money, no food, and I couldn't go on like that.
Q. Was he a drinking man?
A. X wouldn't say he was drinking much; it was more gambling; that was enough; after he gambled I don't think he had money enough left for drinks.
I am not sure what all this is supposed to indicate, Mr. Chairman, but it would seem to me that in this case no consideration was given to reconciliation. I would think many serious matters were involved here, including the problem of gambling, which possibly could have been corrected by sending this couple to a competent family court with all the facilities that are available to such a court. It does not seem that anything in particular happened when the husband left, but that certain developments took place over a period of time and when he finally walked out she did not know whether he was just going out for the evening or was leaving her. I think some help could have been given to this couple during the period of the break-up if they had been sent to the proper authorities.
I am not sure whether it is too late, Mr. Chairman, but I think we in the House of Commons should have the right to ask these people to appear before a competent welfare agency or family counsellor. We should not be restricted just to asking whether they would be able to get along, as was done in the Senate, but should be able to suggest that they do something positive to make a success of this marriage if it is at all possible.

This young lady has been working for an insurance company. I do not know how much she is paid, but if we say she gets $50 a week I am surprised that she has had enough money to pay for a divorce. I presume she has been separated from her husband since 1951, although it does not say exactly when, but I am surprised that she has been able to save enough money to take action for divorce when she has had to look after two children and feed and clothe them, on the salary she has earned in the last three years while she has been working for the insurance company. It would seem to me that it might well be that some further assistance is being given her to enable her to secure a divorce, and that that assistance may be in the form of a settlement from her husband, though that does not appear in the evidence. The youngest child must be eight years old, and it would seem to me that she would need additional help before she could raise the $2,500 that it is reported most of these divorces cost. I would suggest that in this case there was some arrangement or agreement.
As to the actual adultery charged, one of the investigators was Kal Wiseman, age 32, of Montreal. He and his partner followed the gentleman for some time from his place of employment, Dominion Oilcloth Company on St. Catherine street. With relation to the particular day in question there is the following in the evidence of Mr. Wiseman:
Q. Have you ever met the petitioner?
A. Yes.
Q. Where?
A. In your office.
Q. When?
A. It was August of last year.
Q. Where did you go with the petitioner?
A. Went down to a place of employment of her husband, Dominion Oilcloth, on St. Catherine street east.
Q. Do you know the cross street?
A. I believe it is DeLorimier.
Q. Could you tell us what time that was?
A. It was late afternoon.
Q. Did you see the person-
A. She pointed out this one to me.
Q. And she gave you that photograph?
A. Yes.
Q. What happened on September 16?
A. On September 16, through previous investigation I knew that the respondent, Mr. Mazurette, was living with a woman other than his wife as a common law marriage, at St. Christophe street. My associate, Mr. O'Neil, and myself, went into their apartment-call it that, on St. Christophe street, on September 16 in the evening, knocked on the door: it was answered by Mr. Mazurette. Explained to him who we were, and what we were there for. He was most co-operative, was most secretive, as far as he was concerned.
Stopping there, it would seem to me very surprising that a person could be secretive and co-operative at the same time. If you rap on somebody's door and they are co-operative
Private Bills-Divorce
I do not think they would be very secretive. If they were very secretive I think they would shut the door again.
This, Mr. Chairman, is the type of evidence we receive continually from private investigators. In the main I would suggest that they have no education and no training for this type of work at all. I suggest that most of them give a picture that is given to them in the first	place by	the lawyer who	has beenhired in	the	case.	I think the lawyer not
only briefs the person applying for the divorce as to how to answer questions, but also briefs the investigators as to what they are going to see, what they want them to find. In any event, Mr. Chairman, this witness said:
He was most co-operative, was most secretive, as far as he was concerned. He took us into this apartment, and there was the co-respondent, who was using	the	name	Mazurette, but we	found outher name	was	Marie Leclerc. It was,	you could
call it, a two and a half or three room apartment, bedroom, living room, but the only thing separating the bedroom and living room was a thin drape, I would say a flowered drape, over an archway.
He can call it a flowered drape if he wants to. He is giving the evidence. He remembers everything else, but I would suggest that his evidence is not direct evidence. It is not evidence to which you would give much credit if it were any other type of case, but in these divorce cases it seems that not too much particular evidence is needed. I continue:
Q. What kind of an area would you say this is in Montreal?
A. I would consider it is a very poor area.
Q. What time of the night did you enter?
A. It was after eleven.
Q. Did you go right into the apartment?
A. Oh, yes; he admitted us through.
Q. How many people lived in the apartment?
A. Just the two, as man and wife. She was sitting on the edge of the bed, with a white slip underneath a pinkish bathrobe; I imagine that was the colour in its original state.
Senator Burchill asked these questions:
Q. How many rooms were in the apartment?
A. It is just a bedroom and living room and kitchenette.
By Mr. Cohen:
Q. Describe to the committee what the respondent looks like.
A. Well, I remember one outstanding thing, the way his lips are pursed, as if he had no teeth, but he did have his teeth. He is a middle aged man about 45, slender.
Mr. Chairman, when questions are answered with this type of answer I wonder whether the investigators or whatever they call themselves are half-grade morons or even lower in the scale of mentality; because the answers given by these investigators would indicate, in my opinion, they did not have all their marbles. I continue to quote from the evidence:
Q. Did you stay around very long?
A. We were in the apartment some five or ten minutes but did not stay around because they

Private Bills-Divorce admitted they were living there as man and wife. There was no reason to try to obtain further evidence beyond that point.
Q. Did you look at the bed?
A. Yes, it had definitely been used.
It would seem to me, Mr. Chairman, that in this particular case the grounds established are that a common law marriage eliminates the need for proving adultery. I think people could live together at common law without any adultery being committed. Certainly they could live in the same house or in the same apartment, and this fact in itself would not establish that adultery had been committed. I would suggest that in this case the Senate committee has been quite willing to accept the fact that, because they claim to be living as common law man and wife, the condition precedent to this divorce had been fulfilled.
Further questioning by the committee revealed that the woman could only speak French, but the detective could speak French and she also said that this was her husband. He said, "This is my new wife". Again, Mr. Chairman, this couple claim to be living together as common law man and wife. On the other hand we have the young lady trying to raise two children while working as a secretary or clerk in an insurance company, yet she appears to have enough money to hire a lawyer, hire detectives to embark on an investigation, and apply for a divorce through parliament which is going to cost somewhere in the neighbourhood of $2,500. I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that there has been some arrangement made by the husband for obtaining this divorce, because otherwise I think it is financially impossible for the lady to raise these children and, out of $40 or $50 a week, be able to save enough to pay for this divorce.
If this is true, Mr. Chairman-and recalling that when the investigators went into this second apartment Mr. Mazurette said to the detective, Mr. Wiseman, in French "Well, the house is yours; come on in"-then I think this is an indication that should raise some question in the minds of hon. gentlemen as to whether there was collusion in this particular case. There would seem to be some indication of an arrangement by the husband for obtaining this divorce, and the money must have been forthcoming from him to pay the lawyer and the detective.
If this is true, is it not time the committee gave some consideration to the passing of these divorce bills because people set themselves up to live at common law as man and wife? This should be the grounds for the divorce, rather than asking people to fake or to indicate that adultery has been committed. This should be a second ground for divorce, and we should consider it so. If

people are going to admit that they live at common law, then this itself should be grounds for divorce without any other consideration.
Then, Mr. Chairman, I think this divorce should have been granted by reason of the fact the husband had left the wife for a period of seven years. I suggest that in this particular case this could have been grounds for divorce, after the husband had deserted her for seven years and made only a small contribution to the maintenance of the children. This divorce should have been granted automatically because of the desertion over a period of seven years.
I am not sure whether any other hon. member wants to say anything about this bill. I would think all this is an indication that we are granting a divorce for one reason when we should be granting this particular divorce for causes completely dissociated from those established by the Senate committee. I say this because of the co-operation that was given by the husband in establishing the fact that he lived at common law, and on the supposition that he must have contributed toward obtaining this divorce; otherwise I think it would have been financially impossible for the wife to raise the money. I suggest, therefore, that in this particular case we should give some consideration to granting this measure of relief on the grounds that the husband has publicly and openly declared himself to be living at common law with somebody else, and is not the least bit interested in a reconciliation, even if that were contemplated.

I will attempt to deal with some of the more down to earth statements of my hon. friend, but I shall not attempt to follow him on his periodic jumps beyond cloud nine. The fact is that nine years ago this man deserted his wife. She had the care of two children in the intervening time. We should not be surprised that she is able to finance this divorce through parliament when we think that undoubtedly she has been saving for about nine years so she could obtain justice and the right to start a new life, after scrimping and saving while looking after these children for nine years with very little help from her husband.
However, when her petition comes before parliament requesting help this hon. member of the C.C.F. party says the request should be turned down. He said that half-way through his speech, but I realize at the end of his speech he was saying that the divorce should be granted for some other reason than that set forth in the petition. I was not able to follow his reasoning there. It seemed to me he did so many figure eights, twists

and turns, that it was difficult to follow him except that he wanted to see a certain amount of time pass before we could pass this bill and get on to another one.
Now, what are the points to which a reply should be given? It should be pointed out to the hon. member that this system of divorce does carry a disability in so far as maintenance actions and elementary actions are concerned, in that they must be considered in provincial courts, whereas the dissolution of the marriage is to be considered in parliament. The advantage when a provincial supreme court can proceed with divorce jurisdiction is, of course, that you may deal with all the matters under one roof or before one judge rather than, as in this case, having to go before a provincial court and then having to go before parliament. It is, however, true that the woman apparently has made no effort to go into a provincial court in order to extract payment from her husband on behalf of herself or on behalf of the children, but that does not debar her from exercising that right at some future time if she desires to do so. The man's obligation toward his children would exist even though we granted the divorce.
My hon. friend has also made some suggestion that there could have been collusion here, that the husband was rather willing to open the door to allow the detectives in. I suppose after several months of liaison with this other woman and after nine years less two weeks or four weeks of being away from his own lawful wedded wife, he had no particular feelings on the matter. There is not a jot or tittle of evidence, apart from far-stretched inference from what the evidence says, that there was any arrangement between the couple for her to sue him at this particular time. As I say, the desertion happened nine years ago. We have many similar cases in which wives have been deserted or husbands have had a right of action, but because they are poor they have had to save for years and years before they can come here. I hope we do not hear too many suggestions that when the unfortunate people of the world, the really downtrodden people of the world, find themselves in this situation after having saved and spent a considerable amount of money, and their hopes having been raised, we tell them there is hope for reconciliation, that they may yet be able to save a marriage that broke down nine or ten years ago.

I did not intend to make any comments about this matter myself, but inasmuch as my friend the hon. member for Halifax has engaged in this realm of fantasy and has gone further into it than my
Private Bills-Divorce
friend the hon. member for Timiskaming could possibly go, I think it is worthy of comment.
The sponsor of the bill made some reference to saving, scrimping and penny-pinching on behalf of the petitioner in this case in order to finance this particular divorce action through the Senate and through this house. Unless the hon. member for Halifax has some private information which is not available to the rest of us, I would point out that there is not one thread of evidence before the committee to that effect. There is no evidence as to how this is to be financed, where the money is to come from, how the young lady got it or how she is to get it.
Does the hon. member want an answer to that question now?

This is not a question of scrimping and saving; it is a question of interpreting what might be done within the evidence. Even if this is a fact, then it is all the more reason, I suggest, why we should take steps to disengage ourselves in the House of Commons from the consideration of this particular case with which we are dealing and all other cases of this nature. Certainly if the House of Commons were to relinquish what is presently its function in considering this particular case which is before it and others like it, I am sure the cost would be much less. If jurisdiction were altered so that neither section of the parliament of Canada had anything to do with the matter of divorce, the cost would be that much less.

If I may I should like to answer the point raised by the hon. member for Skeena. He says I made my remark without a jot or tittle of evidence to support it. I would refer to page 10, at the bottom of the page. There he will find this question:
Q. Did you ever discuss divorce with your husband?
A. No.
Unless he is going to say that she is telling a lie under oath, I think he will have to admit that the further inference from this is that no arrangement was reached between husband and wife. Another question and answer read as follows:
Q. Who is paying for this divorce?
A. I am.

With respect, may I say to my hon. friend that this proves absolutely nothing. The question and answer are there, certainly:
Q. Did you ever discuss divorce with your husband?
A. No.

Private Bills-Divorce
And when she is asked who is paying for the divorce, she says that she is. It is not a question of drawing from that question and answer that she herself has been saving, scrimping and penny-pinching for nine years in order to finance the cost of this particular divorce. The situation is merely as I suggested, namely that my hon. friend is in the realm of fantasy if anyone is, and is reading into this evidence something which it is not possible to read into it.

The house in committee on Bill No. SD-21 for the relief of Shirley Evelyn Ellis Bertram-Mr. McCleave-Mr. Flynn in the chair.
On clause 1-Marriage dissolved.

In discussing this particular bill I hope my friend the hon. member for Halifax and I do not get engaged in too many differences of opinion in interpreting what the evidence says or misconstruing what the evidence says. There is some indication in the evidence given here in connection with Bill SD-21 in which professional type investigators are involved. I use the word "professional" in so far as their activities in this case are concerned and because they also, from reading other evidence, have participated in other instances involving other people. I hope you will allow me to make reference to this matter even though it is outside the scope of this bill.
There is one serious situation existing here which I think should make us wonder, in our consideration of these particular bills, just whether we are doing the right thing in granting a divorce when from the evidence submitted to a committee of the other house we find that the evidence presented by the investigators was obtained by illegal means or by illegal entry, and by what I consider to be an infringement upon the rights of

citizens of this nation. It is true that some of the individuals concerned in this particular case may have a cause of action of their own for infringement of these rights, but I suggest it is well worth our while to consider this particular question of the invasion of the rights of individual citizens, or the infringement of those rights by these investigators who investigate these particular cases and who investigated this one which is now before us. I suggest that some civil or criminal charges can be laid against these people for the things they did in this particular case in order to gain the evidence to prove what they desired to prove.
In this case I should like to make reference to a few of the questions and answers in the evidence. At page 11 thereof Mr. Kal Wiseman appeared and testified as a witness on behalf of the petitioner. He was asked certain questions by Mr. Cohen, who was counsel for the petitioner. I do not intend to read all the questions and answers but just the relevant part. It is about two thirds of the way down the page. Questions were asked by Mr. Cohen as follows:
Q. Can you tell us what happened on the 28th March, 1959?
A. On that date I had followed Mr, Bertram to the residence of Miss Foreman at 3600 Ridgewood and seen him enter the apartment, I waited out there for several hours and he did not come out. I then called my associate, Mr. Wiseman, at home, about 1.30 a.m., it was a Saturday morning, and asked him to join me at the apartment. He came down and we then went up to the apartment once again, knocked on the door and after several minutes it was answered by Miss Lorna Foreman.
Q. How was she dressed?
Then an answer is given as to the type of clothing this young lady was wearing, and this is the relevant part, Mr. Chairman:
Q. Was there anybody else in the apartment?
A. We asked her if Mr. Bertram was there and she denied that he was and we pushed our way into the apartment.
Then the chairman of the committee, Senator Burchill, inquired further about this, as reported at the top of page 12. Without casting any reflections upon the hon. gentlemen in the other place, I wonder why they did not pursue this particular phase of it. Senator Burchill asked:
Q. Was she surprised when you pushed your way in the door at 1.30 in the morning?
A. It was very close to 2 o'clock. She was surprised, yes, when she did answer the door, and we asked her if Mr. Bertram was inside, and she was rather surprised then.
Then he reiterates what he did:
We then pushed our way in the apartment and it is so situated as you enter the hallway there is a bedroom right to the left and another one adjacent to it, the living room is right ahead and the kitchen back of it, and we could clearly see the respondent attempting to dress himself as we entered-

Then again he says:
We pushed our way in and identified ourselves-
Throughout the report of the activities of these two gentlemen, the Messrs. Wiseman, the investigators, there are three distinct references to having pushed their way into a private citizen's dwelling. We all know that generally there are two ways of gaining access to someone else's home in a legal manner; one is to have a search warrant and the other is to be invited. In this instance there is no reference to invitation, and certainly no reference to a search warrant being obtained; there is only a reference to force, of pushing their way into the apartment.
Then Mr. Cohen asks another question on page 12:
Q. Did you have any other conversation?
A. No, except to tell him our reason for our being there, and the young lady was a little bit frightened throughout this whole thing.
That is quite an understatement, I am sure. Remember that these are the words of the individual investigator himself, not the words of the young lady to whom he referred as being "a little bit frightened". I imagine she would be if in the middle of the morning two gentlemen pushed their way in through the door, barging in in an illegal manner, contrary to our concept of the rights of individual citizens. I am sure she would be quite upset about the whole process.
I wonder very much, Mr. Chairman, whether we are justified in giving proper credence to the evidence of witnesses who, out of their own mouths and by their own testimony, certified by official reporters of the Senate of Canada, have broken the law in order to gain whatever evidence they needed to prove their case. I do not place too much credence on that evidence. In one way perhaps the circumstances in this particular case were such that they were justified in granting the divorce, but I am terribly upset that such things are allowed to take place and that illegal means of entry are used.
There was no subterfuge. They did not say they had a telegram to deliver, or had to check the water pipes, or use any other spurious excuse in order to gain admittance. They merely knocked at the door and pushed their way in, and beyond shadow of doubt they used force to gain illegal entry to the premises in order to enable them to gain evidence to support the petition of the client these investigators were representing.
In fairness to what I have said I would point out that additional evidence was given by Mr. Hyman Wiseman, the partner of the other investigator to whom I have just referred. He gave evidence substantially the same as that given before about the apartment
Private Bills-Divorce
number, the time they knocked on the door, and so on. He is not quite so definite in his attitude toward pushing. Perhaps this is because the other investigator was in the fore of things and did the pushing while the second investigator just followed, but that is pure speculation. Toward the bottom of page 12 Mr. Hyman Wiseman, having been sworn on behalf of the petitioner, was asked questions by Mr. Cohen as follows:
Q. On what occasion did you see John Bertram?
That is the respondent.
A. On March 28, 1959, at one in the morning I got a call from my associate at home telling me to meet him in front of 3600 Ridgewood, that he thought he had seen the respondent enter the apartment. I went down there and he told me he had just gone in about 9.30 or so. We waited until a quarter to two or 2 o'clock and then we went up and knocked at the door, which was opened by the co-respondent, and we asked for John Bertram and she said there was no John Bertram here. She let us in the apartment I suppose because she was afraid of the noise waking up the neighbours.
I do not know offhand what he supposed or what her reasons were for letting him in the apartment, but I suggest it was because of the approach of the person who was giving evidence and the question of pushing their way into the apartment. I suggest with all respect, Mr. Chairman, that regardless of the merits of the evidence in this case meeting the rules as established by the other house, which rules must be met in order that a divorce may be granted, and especially because in this case I understand there are no children involved-an overriding factor which I think we should bear in mind-we should very seriously consider whether we should allow private investigators to use illegal means to contravene the law and people's rights. By our passage of this type of bill without too much discussion about it, or even after a considerable amount of discussion, we are condoning this sort of thing, and I suggest we really cannot allow a continuation and worsening of this state of affairs with the consequent disdainful attitude of investigators who, being professionals, know all the tricks of the trade and what they can and cannot do.
In this instance I think we should discuss quite thoroughly what I consider to be the illegal means of gaining entry-the lawbreaking activities-of people of this nature in order to gain evidence to support a petition for divorce. I for one would think that in this instance this committee might well ask for a review of this case. By this I do not mean that they should inquire whether any facts have been proven or disproven as far as meeting the test of adultery is concerned- as it was explained to me I think that test

Private Bills-Divorce
is met in this case-but this committee should ask our miscellaneous private bills committee to review this particular case.
I am not casting any reflections on the members of this committee, because I know they are very seriously overworked with the volume of business they have to do. We should ask the committee to review this case. The investigators should be called before the committee to explain why they find it necessary to use illegal means to gain entry and should be reprimanded for doing so. Unless the committee does this we will have a repetition of this practice. We know that illegal entry is gained in many of these cases.
A young lady would be reluctant to open her door to a stranger at two o'clock in the morning and would only open it a crack. Presumably, then, the door is pushed in her face and someone forces his way into the apartment in order to gain evidence for use in a divorce case. Unless steps are taken to prevent this practice we will in effect be condoning the use of illegal means to gain entry to premises. If this becomes public knowledge what is to stop a criminal or potential criminal from posing as an investigator and using the same means to gain entry into premises wherein he might steal or commit other crimes?
We should refer this back to the committee in order to reprimand the investigators who are openly breaking the law in gaining entry illegally and who feel they can go without punishment for doing so. The divorce mills in Quebec and Newfoundland have been in existence for so long that these investigators think they can get away with murder.
This would be a good time to adopt this approach. I do not intend to move a formal motion in this regard at this time. In the first place I do not know if it would be in order and in the second place I do not think it should be done in that way until we have had an opinion from other hon. members concerning referring this back to the committee.

Clause agreed to.
Preamble agreed to.
Title agreed to.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Private Bills-Divorce
that I can say about it is that inferences are being drawn for which there does not seem to be any basis in fact.
Then, the following questions were asked:
Q. Did you have any conversation in the apartment?
A. The conversation was. I explained the reason of our intrusion, and this girl asked him what was the trouble. He said it was his wife again causing trouble for him again.
This would indicate to me that the detectives had been there before and that they had some conversation before. The detective points out the girl said that his wife was causing trouble again. This could mean one of two things. It could mean that the wife had been around to visit this gentleman when he had the girl with him or that the detective had been around to visit the gentleman when the girl was with him or, at least, he was around some time in the near past. I would suggest that if the wife was there and had been around raising a fuss, she would not have been able to give the answer that there was no opportunity, as she said on page 10, for reconciliation. If she were around raising the dickens with the husband, then she must have considered that reconciliation was possible.
I am just wondering, Mr. Chairman, how many times can they make this type of entry? How many times do they just keep hounding a guy over a period of time until they find him in a situation that they feel will be acceptable as evidence to the Senate and the House of Commons? How do they operate? How do they know that at this particular time they will get the evidence and exactly how much evidence they need? If they were in the process of moving-he does not say they were in the process of painting or doing other jobs-I think there could be some justification for the conditions that Mr. Etheridge reported he found on entering this particular room and I think it would be stretching everyone's imagination to ask them to consider that adultery had been committed or that it even seemed to have been.
Turning to the next page, it would seem to me that the detective is drawing on his imagination and is not saying what he saw. He was not warned by the lawyer that he could not make this type of statement. The evidence reads:
Q. What was his reaction to this information?
A. He didn't seem to care.
Then he goes on to say:
They were both definitely setting up dual accommodation in this apartment. It is a new section of the city, two and a half, three room bachelor apartments that couples occupy.
It would seem to me that he is drawing quite an inference. Because two people are

in the apartment and the furniture appears to be in the process of being moved in he comes to the conclusion, not from anything he is told, not from anything he sees, that these people are moving into this apartment and are going to establish a common law relationship there. It would seem that he bases this conclusion on the fact that this is a new section of the town in which young married couples live and therefore if someone moves into a bachelor apartment they must be moving into it for the purpose of setting up housekeeping.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Certainly.
Would the fact that the detective found the man and woman in pajamas perhaps not help him to arrive at that inference?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It would certainly help. In reading the evidence I had not noticed that the man was wearing pajamas.
The middle of page 11.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
It is true that both of them were in pyjamas which would certainly give some credence to the evidence. I was of the opinion that the man was in a pair of grey flannel pants as was indicated a few minutes before. Even so, the evidence would indicate to me that certain conclusions were drawn by this experienced detective that are not necessarily in keeping with what he knew or what he saw or with what would be admissible as evidence. In other words, he is drawing his own conclusions rather than basing his evidence on something he was told or something he saw or something he knew. The other detective in this case gave his version and it was not quite the same. In the evidence there is the following:
Q. About what time did you see him there?
A. At 11.20 when I went to the apartment in company of Mr. Etheridge, when Mr. Etheridge rang the bell, and we heard a woman's voice, Mr. Etheridge told her he wanted to see Mr. Rohr regarding his car, his Plymouth.
We did not get this the first time. Mr. Etheridge said, and I give him full credit for saying it, that he was from the Reliable Detective Agency. But his partner said that he asked something about a car. I continue:
So she said, "Just a minute", and a minute after Mr. Rohr answered the door, and we identified ourselves. We went into the apartment, and inside we found out that there was another woman there, Marlene Fleming.
In reading the evidence, Mr. Chairman, I am not too sure whether he means that there was a third party there but in following along it does not appear to be that way. He

obviously knew there was one woman there because she said, "Just a minute", and a minute afterwards Mr. Rohr opened the door. Anyway, if there was another woman she must have stayed in the background because she does not enter into the picture again.
It would almost seem to me, that in these divorce proceedings a pattern is established that the divorces are by agreement, by collusion. In most cases it would seem that there is a certain amount of agreement between the two parties. I think that in many cases, particularly this one, if the people want a divorce they should be granted a divorce. But I think we in this committee should have the right to point up and highlight the evidence given by these detectives. If a detective has proper evidence I think that should be indicated and if he has not I think that also should be indicated.
We should also have the right to decide what payment will be made to the injured party in these cases. If you are a woman, property rights are very difficult to maintain in the province of Quebec and I think we should ask for the right to award damages and allowances to the injured party so that they will not be left destitute when we grant relief. I do not necessarily mean that the damages would be paid to the party who applied for divorce but that in some cases they would be paid to the party who appears to be paying for the divorce, and in most cases this must be the man.
I should like to ask the sponsor of the bill if the miscellaneous private bills committee gave full consideration to this divorce and if by a majority decision they came to the conclusion that the facts as disclosed by the evidence heard before the Senate committee were acceptable to them.

I will answer yes although 1 do not know if one is permitted to deal with any divisions that may occur in the committee. However, the answer is yes. The decision was unanimous. My friend made two points with which I should like to deal. I think one of them was an unintentional slip of the tongue. The other point I wish to draw to his ittention is that the woman herself is work-ng for an insurance company.

The house in committee on Bill No. SD-23, for the relief of Barbara Steinberg Shapiro- Mr. McCleave-Mr. Chown in the chair.
On clause 1-Marriage dissolved.

I had intended, initially, to pose a question or two for the hon. member for Halifax, the sponsor of this bill. However, I shall leave that until later. This is an instance in which there was a child born of the marriage which we are asked to dissolve. Naturally, inasmuch as there is a child involved, this is one of those cases to which I believe we should give more thought, and consider more carefully what we are doing, than we might possibly do if there were no children involved. Certainly, when two adults, because of the actions of one or both of them, feel that there are grounds for divorce, then there are only two adults involved and, presumably each is in a position to look after himself or herself after the divorce takes place.

However, when there are children involved they are the innocent victims of difficult marital relationships. In these cases I feel we should review, as carefully as we can, just what we are being asked to do, and not act hastily because certainly the children should not be subjected to having to grow up in a broken home if some other arrangement can be made. As I have said, according to the evidence submitted, there was one child born of this marriage and arrangements have been made for contributions toward the support of the child in the amount of $10 per week. No indication, so far as I could find, has been given of any arrangement for financial support of the wife who, at the time this evidence was heard by the Senate committee, was not working, even though she is a stenographer. She indicates that she lives now in the home of her parents and is receiving some support from her father. This undoubtedly is indicated in the support that the petitioner's father would wish to give to the grandchild.
In the evidence submitted by Mr. Etheridge and Mr. Paquette, both of whom are investigators, there is an indication of some difference of opinion between them as to what they saw in the particular place they visited. I suggest also that there is evidence of possible collusion in this case between counsel for the petitioner and the respondent. Whether or not the petitioner has knowledge of this collusion is not determined. In fact, she herself in plain evidence, asked by counsel appearing on her behalf, Mr. A. H. Lieff, Q.C., indicates that she knows nothing whatever about the co-respondent or about the adultery or any part in it. In fact, to put this matter more clearly, I should like to refer to the evidence at page 10 where we find the following:
Q. Do you know anything about the adultery to your own knowledge?
A. No, I do not.
Q. I see. Do you know Collette Vigeant?
A. No, I do not.
Q. Is there any agreement or understanding between you and your husband to get this divorce?
A. No, there is not.
Q. Did you scheme about the adultery or plan it?
A. No.
Q. Did anybody plan it for you?
A. No.
Then they go into the question of reconciliation, forgiving the husband and so on, which is not germane to this question of whether or not there is any arrangement or collusion in which the petitioner herself was involved. But I suggest that later on evidence is given which indicates that one of the investigators, namely a Mr. Etheridge, did have knowledge of what was about to occur. As the evidence will show, and as I intend

to relate thereon, the respondent whose name is Abraham Jacob Shapiro was also a party to this arrangement of providing a condition whereby they could prove that if adultery did not take place, at least the condition to such that it could have taken place. If collusion was entered into-as I submit it was- then I am quite sure that adultery did not take place, if the normal course of events is followed in these instances.
Let me indicate from page 11 of the evidence what is the situation. Mr. Ernest Gordon Etheridge appeared as a witness on behalf of the petitioner and, having been duly sworn, testified as follows. Then he was asked questions by Mr. Lieff, Q.C. To lay a background, Mr. Lieff asked some preliminary questions:
Q. Mr. Etheridge, I would like you to take a look at a photograph which has been filed as Exhibit 2. Can you identify that person?
A. That is Joseph Abraham Shapiro.
Q. Did you investigate his behaviour?
A. We did. Our services were retained by Mr. David Notkin, a Montreal attorney, during the month of October, 1959.
Q. What did you learn?
A. As a result of the investigation-we had followed him on previous occasions. He had been living at 3945 Plamondon street.
Q. In what city?
A. Montreal. He was working at the Aldor Door and Window Company at 1111 D'Argenson street in Montreal. He was driving a 1955 Pontiac, licence 151422, Quebec, 1959 licence. On Tuesday, November 3, 1959 we, Paquette and myself-
Incidentally, Paquette is the other investigator.
-took up surveillance at about 5 o'clock when we found his car was parked alongside the company.
That would be the company for which he worked.
He came out and drove uptown. He left his car at a parking lot across from the Chez Paree on Stanley street. He and the woman I had seen him with on one previous occasion left at about 20 after 8. They drove out on Upper Lachine road with the intention of-
Then he was stopped. Mr. Lieff is a fairly sharp lawyer and I am sure he would not want this witness to go on and indicate what was the intention of the respondent.
Would my hon. friend permit a question?
Certainly.
Might not the lawyer have been preventing him from giving hearsay evidence or evidence that was not admissible? You are not allowed to give evidence of intentions or beliefs.

It may well be that is what Mr. Lieff wanted to do. But it is quite apparent what Mr. Lieff wanted to do. The witness said:

They drove out on Upper Lachine road with the intention of-
He did not say "possibly with the intention of" or "what I think might have been the intention" or "what someone later on told me was their intention" or "what, as a result of our investigation subsequent to that time we came to the conclusion was their intention". Oh, no. He said:
They drove out on Upper Lachine road with the intention of-
We find there clear evidence without any question at all that Mr. Etheridge knew at that time what they were going to do because, I suggest, he was a party to it. He was quickly interrupted, as is shown by the next question:
Q. No, no; let us not talk about intention. What did they do?
That is the question by Mr. Lieff. We all look with suspicion upon cases such as this which involve hotels, motels or places where one can stay for one evening only. Where a person has a permanent domicile, such as is the instance in other cases, where a person -man or woman-is there and someone of the opposite sex visits there and stays overnight, you can assume that the arrangements are probably more down to earth and that there is more stability to the arrangement between the particular couple than there is where a motel or hotel is involved or some other equally suspect place.
In all the discussions or things that have been written with respect to collusion in divorce-and it is involved not only in one province but, I submit, all across the country -any indication that is given as to the collusive ways in which divorce can be arranged, they invariably involve hotel rooms, motel rooms and things of that nature and they generally follow the pattern that exists here. One of the parties meets the other of the parties and they drive to an hotel or take a taxi to an hotel or motel and check in. They sign as Mr. and Mrs. So and So, whoever it happens to be. The young lady, whoever she might be, does not disrobe but carries along with her a slip which she puts on over her other clothes in order to make it look as though she has disrobed. The gentleman takes his coat off, loosens his tie and they sit down and wait. After 15 or 20 minutes there is a knock on the door, they let them in, and there is the evidence. Then the so-called husband puts his coat back on. The girl takes off her slip which she has had on over her other clothes and puts it in her purse and they leave the hotel.
That is the pattern that is followed where motels and hotels are involved-as I have been informed by those who have studied

Private Bills-Divorce
the matter and know more about it than do I-where one registers, these are the cases where collusion is more likely to exist than in others, especially when one of the investigators involved in the case, before they get to what motel is used, starts to tell the court what the intention was. I submit that what he was going to say was this: they drove out on Upper Lachine road with the intention of checking into a motel, and so on. How far he would have gone into that matter, I do not know. In any event, he says what they did do which I submit is what Mr. Etheridge knew they were going to do. He said:
A. They drove into the Belvedere motel where there was a No Vacancy sign, and they came out of there and went back to the West End motel, 6700 Upper Lachine road. At about 10.45 we noted that a tray of food was delivered to unit No. 11, and at 11.20 the motel was in complete darkness. Shortly before midnight we went to the door of motel unit No. 11, knocked on the door several times, and he finally opened the door.
Q. Who did?
A. Mr. Shapiro. Once we were inside we identified ourselves to him.
Now comes some dispute as to what existed in the room between Mr. Etheridge and his partner, Mr. Paquette. They are questioned by Mr. Lieff as reported on page 12 as follows:
Q. How many beds were in the room?
A. There was one bed in the room. There was a little cot at the side with a green spread on it which was not used-
This would indicate that there were two beds in the room apparently, although he answered that there was one and then there was a little cot at the side with a green spread on it which was not used. We do not know from that whether none of the beds was used or whether the one bed he talked about was used or the little cot which he said was not used. We do not know what he was talking about; but in previous evidence he said there was a double bed being used. Mr. Etheridge's partner said there was just one double bed and there was not this additional cot, although I suppose it is easy to make that error. Certainly if they made a sketch plan, which is what they said they did, they would have known. He is asked, as reported on page 13:
Q. Did you make a sketch?
A. We made a sketch of the place, and he told them-
I suppose the "he" is the partner, Mr. Etheridge.
-that Mrs. Shapiro was taking a divorce against him and we left.
Q. At what time did you leave?
A. It was around midnight because we went in there at 11.50.

If they made a sketch of the place I am sure they knew whether there was one bed or two.
There is an indication, I submit, of what could very well be collusion between Mr. Etheridge, the investigator and the respondent. In addition to that there is the question again of the rights of citizens. It indicates how the professional divorce mill operators over the years have completely disregarded the rights of individual citizens. In this case they attempted to find out the name of the co-respondent. She was in bed pretty well covered up over the head, and he was asked to proceed in his own words. He went on:
Mr. Etheridge asked her her name, and she said- no, she refused to say her name so he said: "We will find out", and he-
"He" meaning Mr. Etheridge again.
-started to go through her purse

I submit this is another invasion of the rights of people by this kind of investigator who lives off the misfortunes and difficulties of people who cannot because of the existing divorce law take proper and decent steps to have certain conditions recognized. He wanders in in the middle of the night and goes through somebody's purse to find out who she is. I submit that is a gross violation of the rights of the individual, to have one's belongings checked through by one of these types of people I am talking about. If it were a policeman with a search warrant properly authorized by a court to make this sort of investigation, then he might be within his rights, but not when he is in fact just another citizen walking in and proceeding to go through somebody's purse in an attempt to discover just who that particular person is.
This is another instance where we should not take this sort of action lightly, on the part of Mr. Etheridge or anybody else of his kind who are willing to do almost anything to obtain their evidence, including breaking and entering and rifling people's purses. I am sure you, Mr. Chairman, as well as I, know that many married couples consider it a most inviolate thing for the husband to look through his wife's purse or for the wife to look through her husband's wallet. What she puts in her purse is her business and is sacred, and in many cases the husband will not look at it. But this chap here thinks a woman's purse is something he can paw through, and on this occasion he said he was going to look for her address.
There is an inclination, as I related before, for people who have studied this question more thoroughly than I to say that where hotels, motels and so on, are involved a

certain practice is followed, and that when adultery does not take place there is no intention on the part of either party that it should take place. The appearance of the two parties here coincides pretty well with what those who study the problem say traditionally occurs. I again read from the evidence of Mr. Etheridge, on examination by Mr. Lieff, his counsel:
The woman, when I told her the reason for our intrusion, took the sheet from off the top of her head when she heard the words that his wife was going to sue him for divorce. We could see she was lying on the far side of the bed, and she' had the straps of a slip on, and we could see that the near side of the double bed' had been previously occupied. He had come to the door wearing his shoes and grey pants only.
This is the traditional situation. The corespondent in these cases wears a slip. If she wears a sweater it may be removed but she wears a slip and that indicates she is in a more advanced stage of undress. She is covered up to the neck so that the investigators who arrive on the scene can say that they saw certain conditions existing, which is supposed to be the evidence. The man is dressed in trousers, boots or shoes, sometimes with his shirt on and sometimes not, indicating that he is close to the stage of undress and that adultery could have taken place. All they desire is to prove, because they have to prove it, that a condition exists which might well lead us to reasonably assume that adultery had taken place when in fact there may be no desire-or there may be desire but no intention-that adultery should take place. That is especially so on the part of the co-respondent, because generally this is some means of adding to her income and she is not concerned with extracurricular activities of that kind but is solely concerned with having the evidence found and proven by eye witnesses, with someone to collaborate the eye witness, and then they leave and everyone checks out of the motel and they are all happy thereafter.
I suggest that this is precisely the condition which exists in this particular case, especially when Mr. Etheridge leads into it very easily by saying that they "drove out on the Upper Lachine road with the intention of-". I submit it was with the intention of doing what he himself, in conjunction with the respondent in this case, were able to arrange in order that the rules of adultery may have been met to the fullest extent possible so that this house, in considering the case, could say that it met the rules and looked like adultery could have taken place. We are not concerned with whether it did or did not. We are not concerned about whether in fact collusion did take place. All we are 79951-0-1281
Private Bills-Divorce
concerned about is that the proper evidence is submitted showing that adultery might have taken place, but instead we are asked to pass divorces in this fashion. If we are to be asked to do this continuously, we must consider very carefully what we are doing. We must ensure that we are attaching the proper weight to the evidence submitted.
This is the second case in which there has been evidence of the invasion of the rights of individuals. In a previous instance someone made an illegal entry into a place of residence. In the present case there was an attempt or threat to rifle through a purse. We cannot look lightly upon this evidence of gross violation of the rights of individual citizens. These professional investigators who make a living on the unfortunate difficulties of married couples callously forget the fact that people have rights and go to almost any length to gain the evidence they seek.
This case should be sent back to the committee on miscellaneous private bills. I do not cast a reflection on the committee of the whole or on the committee of the other place because with 500 or 600 divorce bills to be rammed through it is difficult for them to thoroughly examine each case.
On the face of it there appears to have been collusion and the rights of an individual were violated in the unholy rush on the part of the investigators to get evidence. The miscellaneous private bills committee should welcome the opportunity of clearing up this question. If it is left hanging fire a reflection is cast on the inspector which suggests that he did something illegal. His name would be cleared if additional evidence were given. Perhaps he made an unfortunate choice of words in giving evidence, although I think it goes further than that.
We should take steps to make it known that this type of conduct will not be tolerated by this committee. Our action would serve as a warning to other investigators to be careful in the future about the manner in which they gather evidence.
I should like to hear the comments of the hon. member for Halifax who has a vast knowledge of the functions of the committee, of the rules as they apply to these cases and a vast concern, shared by me, not only for the welfare of the individuals concerned but for the rights of others.

Mr. Chairman, these matters may be taken up and it may be decided to send for the detectives to deal with the encroachments upon human privacy.
I should like to know if the hon. member was suggesting that Mr. Lieff might be a party to collusion, not that he was but that

Private Bills-Divorce he might have been? If the hon. member replies in the affirmative I would go on to make a very brief statement on that point. I do not care what the hon. member says about the detectives. He can tear them inside out and I will not attempt to defend them no matter what statements are made. However, Mr. Lieff is a very respected lawyer. He would not enter the case until very late, that is after it had gone through all the documented stages and had come to Ottawa. Mr. Lieff comes from Ottawa, not Montreal, and could not possibly have been a party to any collusive scheme.

Mr. Chairman, the only
reference I made to Mr. Lieff was that he was defence counsel for the petitioner and very sharp on the uptake. When the detective began to testify as to his intention, Mr. Lieff interrupted immediately and told him to testify as to facts.
The only reference I made to collusion was between the investigator, Mr. Etheridge, and the respondent, Mr. Shapiro. I had no intention of suggesting that Mr. Lieff was involved in any capacity other than counsel. I did not intend to convey the impression that he was involved in a collusive action and if I did so I constructed my sentence incorrectly.
I raised the question about the committee reviewing this case and if my hon. friend replied I did not hear him. We must have a specific instance for discussion and here we have one. I am not so much concerned about the question of recalling the investigators to inquire about their rifling through a purse. I am more concerned about reviewing the general question of the over-zealous-ness and enthusiasm of these investigators in their attempt to get evidence. I am concerned about the previous case in which they said on three occasions they pushed into the premises.
I would suggest that in the Senate committee, in the committee of the whole, or in the miscellaneous private bills committee of this house, because of its compactness and because of the informality with which it conducts itself and the appearance of witnesses before it, which cannot take place in the committee of the whole, steps should be taken to express our distaste for this sort of attitude or action on the part of investigators. Their actions in this case indicate to me that they have absolutely no concern for the rights of individuals; they have no concern for the law as it applies to the rights of individuals; they will bend, twist or even break the law, which I suggest has been done in this case, in order to gain evidence.


This is what I want to get at. If this is a case upon which we can start such an investigation, upon which we can express our regret, our distaste or our abhorrence for the use of this sort of illegality in gaining evidence, then we should do it. I submit it will do relatively little good to have either here, or in the committee on miscellaneous private bills, individual members express themselves and say, "Well, here is a case where the law relating to private property has been violated by investigators" and let it go at that. Unless we are willing to indicate that we are going to do something concrete about it, I submit that these investigators, because they have been getting away with this sort of illegal action, will look upon it as another voice crying in the wilderness, somebody else in the House of Commons raising this sort of thing. They will say, it will pass over and we will be able to get back to our old practices or malpractices again.
I ask the hon. member for Halifax this question, because of his competence in dealing with these matters by reason of his chairmanship of the committee. Because of his understanding of the problem, will he offer a suggestion as to how we can cope with it and prevent the invasion of the rights of individuals from taking place in the future? I am not concerned about any one particular group of investigators. It may be Mr. Etheridge in this case and somebody else in another case. What I am concerned with is the trend and practice of disregarding the property rights of an individual, the individual citizen's right to privacy and so on, which have been invaded, perhaps even forgotten about or disregarded by the investigators. It is the practice itself I am concerned about.
That can be arranged. There are a number of other cases that will be coming before the committee later on in the session and we can have a discussion on the matter.

May I ask a question? Did I understand the hon. member for Halifax to say that there are other cases which will be coming before the committee? I take it from his remarks he knows, from having read the evidence, which incidentally I have not done yet, that in these particular cases which are to come before the committee there are references to private rights having been invaded, similar to those in this case we are now discussing?
Yes, Mr. Chairman.
That is fine; I will take up the hon. member's offer.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would also like to say something on this point. When you read the beginning of the petition you are surprised to note that in this particular case the couple were married in 1956. They had a child in 1957. In January, 1959, they broke up living together. The sponsor can tell us when they applied for the divorce with which we are dealing today. It would seem to me they did not waste any time in making the application. They agreed to disagree and that was about the size of it. As the hon. member for Skeena so ably pointed out, collusion could very easily have taken place, particularly when it is remembered that this couple probably applied for the divorce six months after they ceased living together.
I mentioned Mr. Etheridge in an earlier case, Mr. Chairman. I said that he was a competent investigator and I still think he is. However, I also think he is a ruthless investigator, and we should give very little consideration to evidence gained in this way. I have been shocked to find that detectives will go to a hotel door or to any other door and try to break it open. They knock on the door; they put their feet in the door; they do whatever they can to gain admittance. They will lie and say that they are the police or they are the desk clerk, or whatever they happen to think of, to gain admittance. I do not think we should accept this type of evidence from that type of person as being legitimate evidence. I am of the opinion that in court a judge or jury would not accept evidence coming from people whom they considered to be of ill repute or had no respect for the law itself. The fact is they asked this lady her name. She did not tell them her name, and I suggest her name was none of their business. Then one of them grabbed her purse and started rifling through it. I agree with the hon. member for Skeena that it is a disgrace. If that is the way they handle investigations in the province of Quebec, then it is about time we put our foot down and said that the rest of us in the other parts of Canada do not like this method of obtaining evidence. We should say we do not have any respect for that kind of thing; we do not believe in evidence obtained in that manner. It is evidence that it not acceptable to us. Those who disagree with us and think it is an acceptable method of obtaining evidence are going to be few and far between. What we are asked to do is to listen to evidence, to admissions made in the manner in which they were made in this particular case.
I think there is good reason to believe that this young couple decided in January, when
Private Bills-Divorce
they did not get along, to get a divorce. They made application for this divorce, I would suggest, before September. It may have been made even earlier than that. I understand that applications for divorce are cut off now. We are working on the new year and one cannot now make application for a divorce to go through this session. Probably this divorce application was made early in the year; it might have been made in March or April. It is certainly true that these people went down to the lawyer connected with this business who put his name on the bill and proceeded to process the divorce. Certainly, the investigator could tell you what the intention of the parties was going to be before he followed them. That is a very good indication that there was a great deal of agreement in this case. When you think that only one or two months could have gone by between the time of the disagreement of the young people and this alleged offence, then you would be justified in thinking that the disagreement constituted collusion, which should have eliminated the possibility of the divorce going through the Senate if they had given very much attention to this aspect of it. This proves that the divorce evidence in this case was not handled properly.
Therefore there would be a period of close to ten months in which some type of assistance could have been given to the couple to warrant reconciliation if the matter had been handled as it would have been in other provinces. If the application for divorce had been made in Ontario the couple would very likely have been sent to a family court to see if the conditions that had caused their separation were not trivial and perhaps the marriage could have been saved with the competent advice of the family court officials.
This is not a case with a long history of disagreement as in other cases we have considered today. A relatively short period of time elapsed in this case before divorce was sought. After the presentation of this evidence I suggest it would be very difficult for Barbara Shapiro to agree to take Abraham Jacob Shapiro back again as her lawful husband. If she believed this evidence then I think that when the senators asked her if there was any chance for reconciliation she would have to say no. But if the divorce had been processed in the proper manner, if divorces were dealt with by the exchequer court as we have suggested on many occasions rather than by parliament-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
