speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was just trying to point out that this particular case is one in which the two parties were separated for a very short time before action was taken for a divorce. It would seem that we either have to come to the conclusion that the woman was not a party to the divorce or she was a party to it. I think there are some grounds for saying that she was a party to getting a divorce. If she was not a party to getting a divorce the fact that the evidence was presented in the manner in which it was would make it very difficult to bring about reconciliation. But if she was a party to this divorce, and it has been suggested that she was, then obviously the conduct that took place in obtaining the evidence would not be sufficient to prevent a reconciliation of the parties even at this late date. It has to be one way or the other. She either knows about the method of getting the evidence and therefore knows that adultery does not necessarily have to take place but only has to be indicated or she believes that there was adultery, and this would indicate that another method should be used for handling these divorces.
I do not know what the decision is with respect to the child in this case. From the names of the people I would assume there is probably money available to maintain the child, but again we are faced with the problem of not knowing what the legal disposition of the child is going to be once the divorce is granted. I think we should have a clear indication in this case by counsel or by someone closely connected with the case before the divorce is granted as to what the intention is with respect to maintenance of the child. If we do not have that then every member of the House of Commons is going to have to bear equally upon his shoulders the moral responsibility, although not the financial responsibility necessarily, to see that this child is looked after in the manner which he would have been if this marriage were not dissolved. This is an obligation that we must all share and I think we must also work toward finding a more acceptable solution so that we will not have to bear this moral responsibility but will know in actual fact what the disposition is going to be.
I agree with the hon. member for Skeena that in this case two of the major faults of these detective agencies are evident. One is the rifling through somebody's private belongings and the second is gaining entry under false pretences, in this case using bodily force. I think that you, Mr. Chairman, as chairman of the committee should give instructions that this case be sent back to the standing committee so that these matters can
[The Chairman.!
be given full consideration. In your office as chairman I think you will agree that enough doubt has been cast on the veracity of the evidence given by these detectives to warrant further investigation of their conduct from the point of view of the rights of citizens and undue invasion of their privacy, and I suggest that you should intervene to send this case back to the committee for further study.

The house in committee on Bill No. SD-24, for the relief of Olga May Hospadaruk Edwards-Mr. McCleave-Mr. Flynn in the chair.
On clause 1-Marriage dissolved.

Mr. Chairman, as a general rule I do not pay any attention to divorce bills. Very rarely do I read the evidence. However, I find this bill somewhat intriguing on several grounds. First, it is a divorce bill from the province of Quebec which does not have any divorce courts. The Senate and the House of Commons have to deal with divorces from Quebec. Second, both the husband and wife declare that they are Roman Catholics. The Roman Catholic church frowns on divorce and does not allow it so it has to be done by the House of Commons because it cannot be done in the province of Quebec. Third, the Christian names of the husband are Harold Edward, and I was rather interested to see what somebody with the same Christian names as myself was up to. I find that his wife is charging him with adultery.
I have read the evidence, Mr. Chairman, and I should like to have some clarification as to what the law is in Canada. Is adultery ground for divorce or is intent to commit adultery ground for divorce? After reading the evidence given before the Senate committee I can find no evidence of adultery although the wife maintained in the committee in answer to a question that she was asking for a divorce on the ground of adultery on a certain date.
You will understand in a few minutes, Mr. Chairman, why I am asking whether the House of Commons grants a divorce on the

ground of intent to commit adultery or on the ground of adultery because if this man committed adultery he is a mighty fast worker. What do we find from the evidence on which the Senate has based its recommendation? We find that at 11 o'clock-oh, no, before that we find that the investigator is asked this:
Q. Do you remember the night of January 9, 1959?
A. Yes.
Mr. Chairman, do you remember the night of January 9, 1959, and what happened that night? There is no evidence before the committee-and this happened over 12 months ago-of any reference to notes. This is a transcript of the evidence, and it says-
I	want to read this very carefully.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Are you speaking to the committee or talking to yourself?

I want to check the exact citation. Here it is:
Q. Do you remember the night of January 9, 1959?
A. Yes.
Q. What if anything happened on that occasion?
Then away he goes. Can anybody remember what happened last week, even, without reference to any notes? There is no reference here to indicate how he remembers what happened that night. Then this investigator says that this man, Harold Edward Edwards was in the York hotel lounge room at 11 o'clock at night. After 11 this investigator saw him leave the lounge room, go to the desk clerk and apparently arrange for a room. He came back into the lounge room, and he and his girl friend finished their drinks. Then they went up to room 311 in the York hotel. The investigator then says he went down into the lobby and "called my man". This investigator and his man then break into room 311 at 11.30 and find the man in shorts and the woman in bed. On this evidence they find the man guilty of adultery.
I say if a man was finishing his drink after
II	o'clock, and with his girl friend goes up to the room which was broken into at 11.30, then he has been found guilty of intent to commit adultery but not adultery-otherwise, he is a mighty fast worker. This is not grounds for divorce, as I understand the law in Canada, otherwise there would be a lot more divorces than there are now.
In addition to that, although the wife says she is asking for this divorce because of adultery on this date, you will also note that the investigator forced his way into the room, and on page 11 of the evidence the investigator says:
I followed them; they went into room 311. I went downstairs to the lobby and called my man.
Private Bills-Divorce
I imagine that "my man" is the one who later gave evidence, a man by the name of Joseph Spevack. These questions were put to him:
Q. What is your name?
A. Joseph Spevack.
Q. What is your age?

Q. Where do you live?
A. Montreal, Quebec.
Q. What is your occupation?
A. Salesman.
Since when does an investigator have a salesman as a man on tap in the lobby, but apparently this one did. What did his man say when he was under questioning? You will find that on page 13 of the evidence, as follows:
Q. Please tell the committee what happened when you got into that room?
A. We didn't get into the room.
That is his answer; we did not get into the room. After telling the committee that he did not get into the room, he then goes on to tell how they forced their way into the room after giving a lot of lies as to who they were and Mr. Rosen, the investigator, using a flashlight. They did not find Harold Edwards in bed. As a matter of fact, he was not completely undressed. The woman was in bed, but whether she was dressed or undressed they do not know because the blanket was up to her neck. Then they said that the bed was disarranged. Just look at that claptrap which is supposed to be evidence upon which adultery is proven and the Senate and the House of Commons are asked to break this marriage asunder. Just how stupid can it get?
I say there can be only one answer to this case. There may have been, and undoubtedly was, an intent to commit adultery but for this evidence to be presented to us as proof of adultery is absolute nonsense. Perjury was committed by both investigators in giving evidence because, in answer to the first question, one investigator said, "We did not get into the room", and two seconds later is telling how they forced themselves into the room. They found the man still had his shorts on and they do not know whether or not the woman was undressed because the blanket was up. This is twenty minutes after the couple had finished their drinks down in the lounge of the hotel. When parliament is asked to take up its time with this stuff and to accept this kind of evidence, then surely not only is it time for a change but surely this is the kind of case which should be referred back to our committee so that witnesses could be recalled to give their evidence and some way found of charging them with perjury unless they change their story a little.

Private Bills-Divorce

I listened with great interest to my friend's foray into this field. It was very dramatic and very interesting. In order to assist him in making up his mind about this particular case, I would point out that the couple were alone in the room for at least half an hour-
Will you find that in the evidence, as to the time?

It is not clear as to the amount of time that elapsed between their entry into the room and the subsequent entry of the detectives, although I believe my hon. friend is putting it pretty well when he says about half an hour.

That being the case, I am going to read into the record here the evidence as to time, exactly as it was given, I presume under oath. The evidence of the investigator is as follows:
Q. I suppose they came out of the restaurant and went somewhere?
A. They came out of approximately nine o'clock, took a taxi to the York hotel on Notre Dame street and went into the coffee lounge and sat until close to 11 o'clock. I notice Mr. Edwards leave the table and go to the desk clerk and come back a few minutes later. They finished their drinks and Mr. Edwards and the young lady went upstairs.
This is a few minutes after 11 o'clock.
I followed them; they went into room 311. I went downstairs to the lobby and called my man.
Q. Did your man join you?
A. Yes, he joined me at about 11.30 that night.
Q. When he joined you what did you both do, if anything?
A. We went to room 311.
Q. What time did you get there?
A. Shortly after 11.30.
They were in the lounge a few minutes after 11, and they were up there at 11.30; that is still very fast work.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I would think that the hon. member for Vancouver East has pointed out the fault in this case, as in so many other cases, that there is no proof of adultery. The only proof is intent to commit adultery, but there is no intention of committing adultery with the party with whom he is at the hotel. There are other arrangements. This is only a commercial method of establishing grounds for divorce in Canada.
Again in this case, as in other cases, it would seem to me that this collusion also has been proved by another fact, namely the fact that the wife could not possibly afford a $2,500 divorce in the House of Commons. As I read the evidence, they have one daughter in this family. The assistance that is paid to the daughter is $10 a week. The wife gets no money at all. I am also aware of the fact that she works and that she earns $50 a week from her employment. If she does this

and if she saves pennies and if she pinches and scrapes by she has $60 a week with which to keep herself and her child. She lives in a place where food is not too cheap, where board also is quite expensive, and where welfare for one person is calculated at something about $40 a week. In these circumstances I would strongly suggest that it is an impossibility for us to consider that this woman has paid the money necessary to hire the lawyers and the detectives and to pay the Senate costs, the House of Commons costs and the cost of producing this bill for the dissolution of her marriage.
The situation certainly fits in with what has been said by the hon. member for Vancouver East, namely that in this particular case, as appears from the evidence, no time was allowed for the committing of this adultery. This is a fact that we have seen established in almost every case we have discussed this afternoon, where collusion must have taken place on at least two or three different counts. I do not know where this woman thinks she got her money or where the detectives or the lawyers think she got this money. But if lawyers are as honest as the sponsor of these bills seems to imply, I think he is going to have to ask himself this question: where did the money come from that is going to pay my bill; where did the money come from that is going to pay the Senate bill. In this case, where we see the opportunity for collusion-
Would my hon. friend permit a question?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Yes.
Did he suggest that I was getting any money for handling these cases? Surely not.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: No. I did not suggest that at all. I should be quite happy if the hon. member could make some money out of them because they certainly involve a great deal of work on his part. No, Mr. Chairman; I am not suggesting that he gets any money. I did not even refer to the fact that he is a lawyer himself. But because he is a lawyer I would think he would know that even lawyers, if they were to ask where the money was going to come from would get some very surprising answers that would not be acceptable in the evidence we have before us. No, Mr. Chairman; by no means do I suggest that the hon. member is getting any money from discharging this responsibility.
Headaches, yes; but money, no.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Experience maybe; but money

no. In this particular case, we again have a problem that has been brought to your attention this afternoon in every other case, outside of this matter of collusion, namely the matter of entry. These detectives do not get into an hotel by the normal manner of coming up and knocking on the door. Without any doubt, you would not get into an hotel room if you went up and rapped at the door. I think every hon. member here should find out for himself whether or not this can be done. All that it is necessary to do is to walk down to the hotel in which you are staying. The next time you go there, rap on three or four doors and you will find out how many of the occupants will open the door when you say you are the desk clerk or something else. I should be greatly surprised if you do not get thrown out a couple of times before you ever get your foot in one of these doors. If you wake somebody up at one or two o'clock in the morning you do not get your foot in the door; you do not get readily admitted.
Mr. Chairman, these people are getting fairly well admitted. In this particular case the detective carried a flashlight which would constitute a fairly good weapon and that would aid in the opening up of that door. They forced their way inside the room. They obtained evidence that is the bare minimum requirement of admissible evidence. In doing this I would suggest they are not operating even within the confines of the law as we know it.
Again, Mr. Chairman, I should like to have your assurance that if we are to pass this bill this afternoon, the daughter by this marriage will be given some assurance that she will be taken care of. It would seem to me that because of the marriage vows people take, they have this built-in maintenance clause for the children of that marriage. By our destroying that marriage contract we are taking away from this child the right it has to maintenance, its right to a good education and its right to the things that either must be provided by law through a separation arrangement or can be given by the marriage contract itself. When we pass this bill this afternoon and there is then no marriage, I think we must assume responsibility, as I have suggested previously, and that we must take upon ourselves the moral obligation to see that financial support is provided to this child until such time as it can look after itself. I think we should do this through the very fact of granting this particular divorce.
You have listened very attentively this afternoon to a number of these cases where these faults are appearing: no maintenance of the children; in some cases no maintenance of the wife; improper action by the detectives 79951-0-129
Private Bills-Divorce
as in this case and evidence that would lead only to the conclusion that collusion has been participated in. I would think it would be an obligation on your part, Mr. Chairman, to bring to the attention of the committee the fact that these things are taking place with respect to the bills that are coming before us and that these bills should all be re-committed to the miscellaneous private bills committee for further study. I think the committee has an obligation to see that these bills get the further study they deserve.

In a moment I am going to add a new proverb to the English language. But first, with regard to the point raised by my hon. friend, may I say that I am not the master of the committee or anything like that. Everybody is equal there. Those who have these points to make can come there and make them, and they should be brought out.
So far as looking after the child is concerned, there is a legal separation and the judgment of the superior court of Quebec ordering the husband to pay $40 a week to the wife. He does not pay it but he does pay $10 a week toward the child. Apparently they cannot make this man pay the judgment of the court, although there are methods by means of which he can be dealt with, for instance, if he were in contempt of court. But legally the situation would be not very much different under a divorce. There is always the opportunity to go back to the court to protect the child. The proverb I was going to make is this: you cannot get blood from a rolling stone.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
You do not want to divorce a rolling stone, either. These are human beings. We are dissolving a marriage. While it is true that further action can be taken in this particular case in the courts of Quebec for maintenance, it cannot be taken by the child. By our destroying this marriage, we are going to be obliged to assume responsibility for this situation, not the court. We are not even sure that the mother is going to accept the responsibility. Normally under the marriage vows these children would be protected. When we have eliminated and made null and void this marriage, as a result of a petition to the House of Commons, we have that obligation. I suggest that until we can function in the manner of a court and make these decisions, we will have to assume the full moral responsibility of the maintenance of these children, and of the wife if necessary. It will be quite a burden on some people if they give some consideration to this fact.
Mr. Chairman, too long have we been able to discuss Bill No. SD-24 and only consider it along with another large group of bills.

Private Bills-Divorce
Now when we do discuss it the remarks oi the sponsor of the bill and the remarks of everyone who speaks in committee are much more to the point because everyone knows what is in the particular bill. I think it is safe to say that these bills came before the committee en bloc, and no reference was made to a particular bill having been a case where forced entry was obtained by the investigator. I do not remember when discussing this bill-I do not remember even if I attended that particular day-what consideration had been given in the Senate to making arrangements for maintenance with the province of Quebec, and discussing whether the courts in that province considered that the case involved a very juvenile ward who would be a ward of the court, and whether because this divorce is granted in the House of Commons it becomes a ward of the House of Commons. It will be surprising how many wards will accumulate if we pass 500 bills. The House of Commons will have to give some consideration not only to this case but to all cases before it where children are left without parents owing to the action taken by this chamber. I am sure no one here will want to shirk their duty in assuming responsibility for this child, or of deciding when the father at least will make payments for this particular child.
These are matters which, it seems to me, we are not considering. We are raising these matters, but a divorce bill is not like a government bill where the minister can stand up and say what he is going to do about it. We are raising these problems of collusion, of improper evidence, of crooked investigators, improper advice from lawyers and many things of that nature, but no consideration is being given to them. The sponsor of the bill is certainly not responsible for all these conditions which exist. He has inherited the conditions over the years.
I think we should sit down and discuss these problems and see if we cannot arrive at some decision before we have to meet a lot of these problems. It would be easier in my opinion to discuss the welfare of this one child of this broken home than to discuss all the children of all the broken homes resulting from all these divorces. With this in view, Mr. Chairman, I would like you to give some direction to the committee, if you so see fit, in order that these matters could be solved in a much more courtly manner than they are at present.
Mr. Chairman, I am providing certain information which will be available to the committee on the exact number of children and wives in the province of Quebec. I think it will be of some assistance.

Mr. Chairman, the chairman of the miscellaneous private bills committee mentioned in this particular case the figure of $40 per week, I think it was, maintenance for the child. I wonder if that order-a court order I presume it is-is to be affected in any way by the dissolution of this marriage?

I think the court order was for alimentary allowance for the wife and child. I do not know the terms of the court order. It might be affected; but the child's right to look to its parent for maintenance, even if there were a divorce, would not be affected by the divorce.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Tomorrow the ten-nation committee on disarmament will start its important work in Geneva. The people of Canada, like those in most parts of the world, have been waiting in hopeful expectation for these discussions to get under way. The house will,

I am sure, expect a few remarks from me about the circumstances in which the talks are to begin.
This evening the five western powers represented on the committee are releasing a paper which sets forth the opening negotiating position of the west. With the consent of the house, Mr. Speaker, I would like to table this paper setting out the initial western negotiating position. Perhaps it could be printed as an annex to today's Hansard.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the house agreeable to having this document printed as an appendix to Hansard?

Agreed.
(Editor's note: For disarmament plan referred to above, see appendix).

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It takes the form of a three stage plan for comprehensive disarmament.
During some six weeks in Washington the western five evolved this plan, last week it was put in final form in Paris and was considered and approved by the NATO council. Hon. members will understand that what has been formulated and announced is an initial negotiating position. This means that it may undergo modification as the negotiations develop, for there could be no negotiating if one side or the other were to stand on a fixed and inflexible position. Canada will urge that the western negotiators continue to seek improvements in an effort to reach agreement with the Soviet side.
While both the western powers and the Soviet union have put forward blueprints for a three-stage program, the proposals of the west do not constitute a package. They call for study leading to agreement on specific measures of disarmament. However, as soon as required studies on many items are completed, the appropriate agreements can be concluded and implemented, whether or not other items in the same stage are ready for agreement. Therefore in areas where it proves possible to move forward to agreement, progress will be rapid and there can quickly be partial measures of disarmament within the scope of the general plan.
I have said that there is agreement among the western powers on the broad lines of the program presented. There have been, and remain, differences of approach and emphasis, just as there are differences of interest and judgment. For example, under instructions, General Burns has pressed to have urgent attention given to measures of nuclear disarmament and he has had some success in this respect, though not as much as I should have liked, in this approach we shared to a degree the views of the French government, whose proposals dealing with the control of 79951-0-129J
Western Proposals for Disarmament the means of delivering nuclear warheads seemed to meet one of the major causes of anxiety in the world today.
Similarly, in our view the items concerning the cut-off in the production of fissionable material for weapons purposes and the conversion of existing stocks to peaceful uses deserve higher priority and should be closely linked with the reduction of armed forces and armaments to the levels proposed.
While these views have found some expression in the western plan, we continue to believe that there is room for improvement. In line with this attitude we welcome the inclusion, early in the western program, of studies and measures designed to prohibit, under effective control, the placing in outer space of weapons of mass destruction.
As it stands, the western position is realistic, negotiable, and offers no threat to the security of any state, it looks forward to an ultimate goal of general disarmament, applicable to all countries with a significant military capability, and effectively controlled through an international disarmament organization. It envisages too, the establishment in stages of international machinery for keeping the peace and for enforcing a rule of law. Appropriate links with the United Nations are contemplated and in the view of the Canadian government this is of great importance.
It would be neither profitable nor desirable to enter the ten-power negotiations, which will be exclusively concerned with disarmament, in the belief that no significant progress can be made until political issues have been resolved. On the contrary, we believe that agreement on disarmament measures can and will help to improve the chances for political agreements. Accordingly, it is our intention to pursue vigorously the objectives of disarmament as such, and to work assiduously for the early implementation of agreements in as broad an area as may be possible.
I believe that it is incumbent on all concerned to view the forthcoming negotiations with hope and optimism. For years the people of the world have been yearning for peace with security and for freedom from anxiety about war. During the past decade and a half we have seen an unprecedented preparation for defence, in a period of great scientific advance, but there has been no increase in security and no decrease in anxiety. If anything, international insecurity has grown and with it an appalling risk of war through mistake or miscalculation. Moreover, nations everywhere have had to bear the crushing burdens of defence with no prospect of relief in sight and with a depressing effect on many economies.

Western Proposals for Disarmament
The time has come to concentrate on steps to be taken towards meaningful disarmament. The political atmosphere of today is as favourable to such action as at any time since the second world war. Canada is participating in the disarmament negotiations believing there is hope for success. We are encouraged by the degree of harmony within the western team and by their serious approach to the subject. They have a determination to achieve results and we hope that this will find response from the soviet side. We will do all we can to assist in this most important endeavour.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps in the circumstances the house would permit me to make a short comment now on the statement we have just heard from the minister.
In the first place, may I thank the minister for his courtesy in sending me, an hour or so ago, a copy of the proposed plan which he has mentioned in his statement and therefore I have had an opportunity to give it at least very cursory consideration.
I agree with the minister that it is encouraging to learn that the western five have an agreed plan for controlled and supervised disarmament. Even cursory consideration indicates that it is one of detailed and far-reaching importance based largely, it would seem, although not entirely upon British and French proposals which have already been made public in essentials.
On the face of it this plan seems to me to provide a good starting point for progress. I am glad that the minister emphasized that it is only a negotiating position which is embodied in this plan but it does provide a good starting point for progress in this vitally important field at the disarmament meeting which is about to open in Geneva. Any such progress at this conference will, I know, receive the support of all Canadians.
It is easy to grow discouraged, even cynical, about the possibility of achieving disarmament in a divided and fearful world. So many attempts have been made in the last 30 years and so many have failed. It is possible, however, to be realistic about this without yielding either to defeatism or despair because that would be fatal, as the minister pointed out, to any chance for success. There is, moreover, a far greater incentive to success now than ever before because the penalty for failure would be so much greater than ever it was.
All history shows that the piling up of armaments has always ended in their use. In the past that has meant devastation and destruction. In the future it could mean global annihilation. Those are the stakes

that face the conference that opens at Geneva as well as the international political discussions between great powers which are now taking place and which will have a bearing on the Geneva conference.
It would be folly, of course, to expect quick and spectacular success. It would be fatal not to work, all of us, with devotion and wisdom and energy to the ultimate achievement of such success. I am certain, as I know all hon. members are, that the Canadian delegation at Geneva will do just that under the instructions they receive from the Canadian government.
The achievement of peace in a world which will have abolished the machinery for its own nuclear destruction is bound to be a slow process but it must be a sure one if man is to survive.
Therefore we all join the minister in praying for the success of the Geneva conference and we wish the Canadian delegation well in the contribution that I know it will make to whatever success can be achieved. The disarmament plan which has been submitted by the five members of that conference provides, it seems to me, a good foundation on which to build toward that success.

Mr. Speaker, although it is after the normal hour of adjournment for dinner, I trust the house will bear with me for four or five minutes while I comment on behalf of this party on this most important question. First of all, I thank the minister for his statement just given to the house, and I also wish to thank him on behalf of this party for his kindness in supplying us with a copy of the text of the disarmament plan, I think about an hour ago.
I am not one who likes to make extemporaneous remarks on these very important questions. I like some times to mull them over. However, I had an opportunity to read through this text and I do wish to make a few comments on behalf of the party for whom I am speaking.
We are glad to know that the conference is going to function in accordance with United Nations principles and action is being taken toward that end. We are glad to know it is going to work out measures leading to general disarmament, we hope, first, as a result of studies of various proposals placed before that conference and, second, as a result of action to implement the measures after those studies.
In that respect we are of the opinion that is a very logical approach. However, we have a few suggestions to make. I want to let the minister know that I make those suggestions

in no sense in a partisan way. I make them in an effort to make our small contribution toward the approach to this most important question.
First of all, let me say that our group regrets that China is not participating at the present time in this conference, or is expected to participate in the near future in the conference mentioned in the text. We urge that every avenue be explored in every way to bring representatives of the mainland Chinese government into consultation with the members of this conference because we believe that without the participation of the government of China, without its inclusion in consultations, and things of that sort, there can be no satisfactory general disarmament plan, and I say that, period.
This party also believes-although I understand that action is being taken by other groups to give some effect to our hopes in that direction-that the question of cessation of nuclear tests is a part and parcel of disarmament. We would like to see some consideration given to that in this text just given to us by the minister. We believe that should be on the agenda of the conference in the future.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This is being handled by another conference in which the United Kingdom, the United States and the Soviet union are participating.

We are very pleased to know that. We have had some information in that respect, but does it mean that these two committees will be working together, or dovetailing their efforts so that the cessation of nuclear tests will be given consideration? I presume that is what the minister means.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Only the one committee; it is the responsibility of the three nations conference.

Then we also ask, is Canada not weakening her position in the discussions and in the discussions on the banning of nuclear tests by making provision at this time for nuclear weapons on Canadian soil? This party is of the opinion it would be wise at the present time, and a worth-while contribution to the morale of the conference and the committee, for us to delay any final decision in that respect.
May I make one or two other comments. I notice that paragraph b of part II has this to say:
Prior notification to the international disarmament organization of proposed launchings of missiles according to predetermined and mutually
Western Proposals for Disarmament agreed criteria, and declarations of locations of launching sites, and places of manufacture of such missiles-
And so on.
We suggest, that this first inclusion, shall I say, of locations of launching sites can be somewhat of a temptation until we have other matters settled, and the balance of terror could, as a result of that order of procedure measures outlined in section 2, create something of a highly unstable condition. We suggest-and we offer this to the minister for his consideration-that paragraph e should precede paragraph b in these proposals. Paragraph e reads as follows:
Establishment of appropriate measures to give participating states greater protection against surprise attack, including aerial inspection, ground observers at agreed points, mobile ground teams, overlapping radar, notification of aircraft flights, and appropriate communications.
We think this paragraph should be placed where paragraph b is at the present time. In particular, we think that to do otherwise is, in ordinary language, to some extent to place the cart before the horse.
These are the few comments I wish to make on behalf of this party, after a very brief and hurried review of this text of the disarmament proposal; but I join with the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Pearson) in wishing the minister every success in all he undertakes in this very important question.
On some occasions the minister has been accused somewhat of being a bit over-optimistic, rather over-hopeful, I think. I am glad to say that the Gazette of today gives us some reason for some optimism and hope. It carries a headline:
Total A-Test Ban Bid By Democrats Scientific Body Offers Police Plan
In the United States there are proposals for a total ban on A-bomb tests, and then there is the appeal for total disarmament made by the minister of science in the government of Great Britain yesterday. These are all very hopeful signs. I support the minister in the hopeful attitude because unless we have faith, conviction and hope our efforts will largely end up in sterility. We must have conviction. I know the minister's conviction; I know his sincerity about this question and on behalf of this party I wish him every success.
In conclusion, let me say that the C.C.F. party hopes and prays that this conference and all those that work together in it will blaze a trail, a pathway to peace for mankind in the days to come.

He said: Mr. Speaker, before the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) speaks, I should like to make a few remarks on the bill. The legislation encompassed by the bill purports to amend the provisions of the constitution of the British Columbia Telephone Company. The company was incorporated by a private act of parliament, namely chapter 66 of the statutes of Canada, 1916. At that time the name of the company was Western Canada Telephone Company but this name was later changed to British Columbia Telephone Company.
This company operates over 90 per cent of the telephones in the province of British Columbia and it is the second largest telephone company in Canada. The scope of the activities of the company is indicated by the fact that at the end of 1959 the company served 505,432 telephones and had a gross investment in telephone plant of over $243 million.
Section 9 of the incorporating act gives to the present company the power to purchase the property and assets of any company having similar objects and the sole purpose of this amending bill is to empower the British Columbia Telephone Company to acquire the shares and to become a shareholder of any company or companies having objects in whole or in part similar to the objects of the British Columbia Telephone Company.
The directors of the company were advised by counsel that section 9 as it now stands does not authorize the company to acquire another company by the purchase of its shares, and hon. members will appreciate that in the acquisition of companies today it is usually much more convenient to purchase the shares of any such company and then to amalgamate its operations with those of the purchasing company.

The company decided to enact a new section rather than to amend section 9 of the incorporating act. Section 10 of the incorporating act provides that sections 153, 154 and 155 of the Railway Act shall apply to the company and to any company which it may acquire under section 9. These provisions are rather cumbersome because these sections of the Railway Act require the approval of the governor in council to any sale, lease or amalgamation, and further require that once any agreement of amalgamation has been approved by the governor in council the companies shall be deemed to be amalgamated and shall form one company.
The proposed amendment is purely technical, Mr. Speaker, because it facilitates the final purchase of the assets of another company by first making it a subsidiary through an exchange of shares. Hon. members can therefore see that this is a facilitating power and it is requested to implement the powers which the company already had under section 9. I might say that the Bell Telephone Company presently enjoys the power which this bill will give to the British Columbia Telephone Company.
I believe the most important consideration of this bill is that the amendment provides for the issue and allotment of shares of the British Columbia Telephone Company in payment of or in exchange for the shares of the company it proposes to acquire. This will permit the company to effect a saving of cash funds which are badly needed to carry on the program of expansion and improvement in its own system. During the coming year British Columbia Telephone Company will acquire $32 million for this purpose of expansion, and the allotment of shares in payment rather than the use of actual cash will, therefore, save the company from having to provide additional cash funds during a period of high interest rates such as exist at the present time.
The proposed amendment provides that no purchase of the shares of another company can take effect until it has been submitted to and approved by the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada. Hon. members might be interested to know that the immediate object of this bill is to acquire the shares of the North-West Telephone Company, which was formed in 1928 to develop telephone communications by radio to the more inaccessible communities along the coast of British Columbia. The North-West Telephone Company represented the first commercial application of the use of radio to provide telephone services in British Columbia's mountainous terrain where it was not economically possible to build or maintain wire lines. Subsequently,

the British Columbia Telephone Company acquired a charter power to provide telephone service by radio, and it is now operating radiotelephone communication in British Columbia on an expanding scale.
For example, the British Columbia Telephone Company, in 1958, completed the British Columbia portion of the trans-Canada microwave radio relay system which means that there is now a microwave system of transmission from Vancouver to Montreal. The North-West Telephone Company is faced with heavy commitments for expansion and improvement in the area served by the company in central a British Columbia. The communities of that area, although widely separated, have experienced phenomenal growth. The necessity to provide telephone facilities to meet this growth has created, and will continue to create, a financial burden which is most difficult and costly for a small company to carry. Increasing interest and dividend rates have contributed substantially to the rising cost of providing and maintaining telephone service, and experience has shown that the issue of securities in large amounts, and the ability to provide a somewhat higher security rating makes it possible for larger companies, such as British Columbia Telephone Company, to attract capital at rates considerably lower than a comparatively small company such as North-West Telephone Company.
As a further source of information, I may say, that during the last 10 years the British Columbia Telephone Company has acquired the Mission Telephone Company Limited; the Chilliwack Telephone Company; the Kootenay Telephone Company Limited, and a large part of the dominion government telegraph and telephone system, and in each case improvements in the service and equipment have been immediately evident. Many thousands of dollars, which the smaller companies could not provide, have been spent in expansion and modernization. These considerations have an important bearing on telephone rates and indicate that the cost of providing service for a small company serving communities in rural areas will rise more rapidly and reach higher levels than those of a large communication system such as British Columbia Telephone Company.
The immediate object of this amending bill, Mr. Speaker, is the acquisition of North-West Telephone Company by the British Columbia Telephone Company, which appears to me to be in the best interests of the subscribers and the public. Once again I say that we should do something to close this gap in responsibility. The situation should be remedied, and I trust that when the bill goes before the committee the members of the committee will take every opportunity to bring this situation to the attention of the officials again and let those officials know that while our efforts to date have not met with success we are going to continue our efforts until they do.

My friend the hon. member for Vancouver Centre referred to this company as a creature of the federal parliament by act of incorporation in 1916. It specifically recognized the fact that this creature might amalgamate or absorb the other large creature that already existed and have its powers, and therefore I feel I must deal briefly with the history of the first creature.
This company had its beginnings in the province of British Columbia under a very old act of incorporation of the legislature of British Columbia. In fact, it was the first incorporated telephone company in all of Canada. I refer to the Victoria and Esquimalt Telephone Company incorporated by chapter 27 of the statutes of British Columbia of 1880. I know that some of my hon. colleagues may say that was the same year the Bell Telephone Company was incorporated. They will ask how I could claim that this company was the first to be incorporated. In answer I would point out that this bill received royal assent on May 8, 1880. The Bell Telephone Company was incorporated later the same year. Therefore the Victoria and Esquimalt Telephone Company was the first incorporated telephone company in British Columbia and covered the southern tip of Vancouver island.
In 1884 another company was incorporated. Under chapter 31 of the statutes of British Columbia of 1884 the New Westminster and Port Moody Telephone Company came into being. It afterwards changed its name to the New Westminster and Burrard Inlet Telephone Company and took over the area that subsequently became the city of Vancouver. The city of Vancouver did not exist when the Victoria and Esquimalt Telephone Company was incorporated. These two companies operated in their areas and then in 1890 under

chapter 66 ol the statutes of British Columbia for that year the Nanaimo Telephone Company was incorporated which operated principally in the central portion of Vancouver island.

In 1891 another telephone company was incorporated in British Columbia under a very strange name which possibly the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) would remember. Under chapter 67 of the statutes of British Columbia of 1891 the Vernon and Nelson Telephone Company was incorporated. We are now going into the interior of British Columbia. I believe I have shown that the southwestern portion of the mainland was covered by two telephone companies and Vancouver island was covered by two, and now we are in the interior.

8.
