5. (1) -The company may construct, erect, operate and maintain a line or lines of telephone along the sides of, and across, or under any highway, streets, public bridges, or any such places in and throughout the province of British Columbia as the company from time to time determines-
The legislature of British Columbia as a result of this amendment gave the Vernon and Nelson Telephone Company the right to operate anywhere in British Columbia.
[Mr. McPhillips.l
That would include the Kootenays, would it not?

Oh yes. Section 8 of the same act is one of those innocuous sections which members of the legal profession put in. These sections do not mean very much unless you understand the references. Section 8 simply states:
8. The provisions of sections 82 and 83 of the Companies Act, chapter 44, Revised Statutes of British Columbia, 1897, shall apply to the company.
Those sections were the sections that provided that the company could change its name. That is exactly what the Vernon and Nelson Telephone Company did. It changed its name to British Columbia Telephone Company Limited. There we had the creature and it was under provincial jurisdiction.
That creature then proceeded to gobble up all the other telephone companies I have mentioned and, as the hon. member for Kootenay West has already indicated, it did not become very popular in the process. There was a great deal of outcry in British Columbia and as a result the directors decided they would hasten to get under federal jurisdiction if they could.
Again we have an act of incorporation in 1916 as referred to by my friend the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. If I may say so without giving any offence, here again the company adopted what I might say was a phony name. The company was incorporated under the name of Western Canada Telephone Company. Section 11 of this statute reads:
11. Notwithstanding anything in this act contained, should the British Columbia Telephone Company Limited be amalgamated with the company and all the undertaking, property and assets-
And so forth. It goes on to say that the company incorporated be substituted in all the contracts. At this point I think I am going to clear up a little mystery for the hon. member for Kootenay West. I refer again to the statute. Subsection (3) of section 11 reads:
(3) When the works and undertaking of the British Columbia Telephone Company Limited are acquired or leased by the company such works and undertaking shall be deemed to be and are hereby declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada.
And so the creature, which has become extremely unpopular as a monopoly in British Columbia, had safely slipped off the hook and under the jurisdiction of the board, as it then was, of railway commissioners for Canada, where 1 think they thought they would be safer.
Now, so far as the continuing power is concerned, section 9-and the hon. member

for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Jung) referred to it-provides as follows:
The company shall have power to purchase, take over, lease, amalgamate with or otherwise acquire from any other company or companies having objects in whole or in part similar to the objects of the company all or any part of the property, real or personal, undertaking, business, powers, contracts, privileges and rights of any such company or companies that may have been conferred upon any such company or companies by charter, acts of incorporation-
Or otherwise; so that by the enactment of the parliament of Canada this company, which is now before us, by the expressed words of the parliament of Canada, was given all the powers of the company with which it amalgamated and, as I have shown, Mr. Speaker, one of those powers was the acquisition of shares in any other company, and the right to issue its own stock in payment thereof.
Why does this company come to the parliament of Canada? I made some reference to the legal advice. But suppose they had received legal advice that they had this power, why are they here? I think they are here for one reason, as the hon. member for Vancouver Centre has indicated, and it certainly was indicated in the debate in the other house. The primary object of this amendment is so that the British Columbia Telephone Company may acquire the stock in North-West Telephone Company. The North-West Telephone Company is not a very well known company. It is a creature of the legislature of British Columbia of 1928. It has radio powers, radiotelephone powers, and it has a licence from the government of Canada to carry on those powers. It is in no sense a subsidiary of British Columbia Telephone Company, as some people think. It was incorporated by the representatives of United States owners of the British Columbia Telephone Company, and their holding company, the Anglo-Canadian Telephone Company of Montreal is a majority shareholder and that in turn is owned by the Associate Telephone and Telegraph Corporation of Chicago.
I think this is just a question of wanting to have your cake and eating it. I think this legislation is somewhat in terrorem of the existing shareholders of British Columbia Telephone Company because, Mr. Speaker, if this plan is put through, the control of North-West Telephone Company is assured to the same United States owners because the stock will be owned by the British Columbia Telephone Company, and, possibly, with those huge earnings that the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), has mentioned, the United States owners of the stock in the North-West Telephone Company can get cash or they can get shares in the
Private Bills
British Columbia Telephone Company, which has a market ability which the shares of the North-West Telephone Company do not enjoy, so that in effect they can have their cake and eat it.
I think I have demonstrated the fact that in essence this company is wasting the time of parliament in coming here and asking for powers they already enjoy in this country, asking it for a purpose, to be able to say to its own shareholders, "the parliament of Canada has just given us this power"; in other words, in terrorem, "you dare not say we cannot buy the shares of that company, the parliament of Canada has given us this power". I think that is the whole proposition and I am very much against it; I am very much against this bill being given second reading.

Mr. Speaker, I am very interested in the bill, and I was particularly interested in the comments made by the hon. member for Victoria, British Columbia.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, I am a native of one of the three prairie provinces where the people do not have the worry and the concern over their telephones that the people of Ontario or British Columbia have, in that in each of the three prairie provinces the telephone systems are owned by the people as a whole and they have rates which are lower than the rates in either Ontario or British Columbia.
The explanatory note of the bill says that:
The sole purpose of this bill is to empower British Columbia Telephone Company-
And so on. I always look askance at any announcement reading that the sole purpose of the bill is this or that, or whatever the case may be. I am saying this now because we are asked to grant greater authority to the British Columbia Telephone Company. I am unwilling at this time to express an opinion as to whether or not on third reading we ought to vote for this bill. I think it will depend on the information we get, and on the manner in which we get it, when this bill reaches the committee stage. It is on this that I would like to say a word or two, because my experiences with this company in that regard have not been exactly pleasant. I can remember how approximately 12, 13 or 14 years ago the people of British Columbia wanted to find out what this company really was, and the public utilities commission of the day held extended hearings in an attempt to get into all the ramifications surrounding the British Columbia Telephone Company, and they finally had to conclude their hearing; they were unable to reach any conclusion

Private Bills
because they found' themselves involved in telephone and in telegraph lines, in cities as far away as Honolulu.
We had a clash with this company a number of years ago when it was asking for legislation for its welfare from the parliament of Canada. At that time the company asked for permission to increase its capital stock. It pleaded that this authorization was essential if it was to continue to have the capital resources necessary to meet the growing needs for modern telephone services of the people of British Columbia. I can remember the difficulty we had with the officials of the company at the committee stage, in that it took them a very long time before they came clean, before they honestly admitted who were the effective owners of the British Columbia Telephone Company. They did their utmost, despite the intense questioning of the then member for Nanaimo, Mr. Colin Cameron, to hide the identity of those who controlled this company. After many long hours they finally had to admit that they were a United States-controlled company.

I should like to ask the hon. member if he would not reconsider his words. I was a member of the same committee and my recollection is not the same as his. I do not think we should be unfair to the company in this matter and I think he is being unfair.
May I say that I believe this happened before the hon. member was a member of the house.
The hon. member only came here in the middle of the year.
November, 1957 was when they appeared before the committee.

They appeared again before the committee at that time. I do not think the hon. member has in mind the same committee meeting to which I have reference. Be that as it may, at that time they were granted the authority to expand their capital structure on their plea that this was absolutely essential if they were to meet the ever-growing needs of the people of British Columbia for a modern telephone system. However, what did they do? Hardly had the parliament of Canada agreed to their plea than they turned right around and greatly raised the rates for service to the people of British Columbia, at the same time using the identical argument that had been used here. They obtained the authority here to increase their capitalization and then turned to the telephone users of British Columbia and said that they regretted that

they had to increase their rates in order to meet interest charges and the earnings necessary because of the increased capitalization.
In order that hon. members may know that we know what we are complaining about, may I say that I have here my latest British Columbia Telephone Company bill. I have only one extension in my house and the bill amounts to $7.88. In my opinion this is unduly excessive and is in part caused by our not having complete authority over our own public utility within the confines of our province. I heartily endorse the attempts of the leader of our party in the legislature of British Columbia to return the telephone company to the jurisdiction of the legislature of the province of British Columbia.
We have been misled on other occasions by this company and when the company asks us at this time for authority to acquire the shares and become a shareholder of any company or companies having objects in whole or in part similar to the objects of the British Columbia Telephone Company we have very great reservations whether or not this move, if it succeeds, will not help to raise our rates higher still. I have very great reservations in that I feel that the existing users of the North-West Telephone Company are not going to receive any blessings by way of a break if this proposed legislation receives the endorsation of the house.
It is for these reasons that we will eagerly await the consideration of this matter by the standing committee. I hope that we will receive immediate, clear-cut and more honest answers from the officials of this company than we have had on other occasions when they have appeared before us.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up very much of the time of the house in talking about this bill. It has already been pointed out that this is a power usually conferred on companies and it has also been pointed out that the operation of a telephone system must necessarily be a monopoly. The hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. McPhillips) has argued with a great deal of legal skill that the company already enjoys this power.
I was rather interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) who feared that this company would become a monopoly owning all the telephone companies in British Columbia which would lead me to believe that the hon. member for Kootenay West must be considering selling his telephone company to the British Columbia Telephone Company because in his introductory remarks he said that he was the president of the smallest telephone company operating in British

Columbia. As long as the hon. member for Kootenay West sticks to his rugged, conservative individualism the British Columbia Telephone Company will not have a monopoly.
The hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) had a lot to say about the operation of telephones on the prairies. This may not be strictly germane to the subject, but I think I should say that I have had some experience with the Alberta telephone system and God save us from the sort of service and type of operation provided by that government system.
On a point of order, would the hon. member explain what he means by that last statement?
You will get more wrong numbers in five minutes from the Alberta telephone system than you will from the British Columbia telephone system in a year.
You have to know your numbers to start with.

The British Columbia telephone system has gone through a period of fantastic growth as exemplified by the number of times the company has come to parliament to ask for additions to its capital. Its capital has increased by successive stages from $11 million in 1940 to $25 million in 1947, $75 million in 1951 and $250 million in November of 1957. These figures indicate the growth of British Columbia and the job which has been faced by this company in meeting the needs of that growth. I defy any member from British Columbia, and I am not talking about rates now, to say that the British Columbia Telephone Company has not done a first-class job in keeping up to the service requirements of perhaps the fastest growing area of Canada. We have had a smaller backlog of unfilled telephone orders than any other place in Canada. As far as I can make out, the company did a better job in British Columbia than the Bell Telephone Company did in this part of the country.
I have no quarrel with the purpose of the bill. I know a bit about the interior of British Columbia. I can think of many places where the operations of the British Columbia Telephone Company if extended to these areas would add something to the telephone service already being provided in the interior. To my knowledge the company has been a good company. If the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam will read the report of the proceedings of the committee of November, 1957 I believe he will find that the company officials were absolutely honest, open and aboveboard and absolutely direct in their replies to members of the committee. When the bill
Private Bills
goes to the committee perhaps the company officials will be given somewhat of a rough time but they are very capable people who will know how to handle themselves and I am quite sure that the committee members will receive answers to all the questions they may wish to ask.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

the second reading of Bill No. S-16, to incorporate Matador Pipe Line Company, Ltd.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is a bill to incorporate Matador Pipe Line Company. Section 1 of the bill which we have before us sets out the applicants. There are two residents of the United States and, as is customary, there are a number of partners in a Calgary law firm, so it follows that Calgary will be the location of the head office of the company if this house sees fit to authorize this incorporation.
The reason or the object in incorporating this company is to transport crude oil, manufactured and refined in North Dakota, 60 miles north to Cromer, Manitoba, thence east to Duluth and Superior and then south into the markets of Wisconsin and Minnesota. Up to the present this crude oil has been transported by tank cars at an uneconomical or what has become an uneconomical price, for a distance of some 200 to 300 miles directly from North Dakota into Wisconsin and Minnesota. It is for the purpose of making an economical delivery from the source of supply to the markets that these applicants are seeking incorporation.
The line will run north, as I said, from a point about eight miles east of the Sas-katchewan-Manitoba border, some 60 miles to Cromer, and then east from Cromer to Duluth and Superior, but at Cromer, Manitoba, it will be linked up with a pumping station which is part of the Interprovincial Pipe Line. As most hon. members know, the Interprovincial Pipe Line Company starts in the province of Alberta and moves east through to Duluth-Superior and then from there to Sarnia and Toronto. It is the connection at Cromer and from there east to Duluth-Superior that this company seeks to set up.
The company is going to raise capital, but I do not think by public subscription. It will have a share capital of 100,000 common shares, without nominal or par value, and
18,000	preferred shares of a par value of

Private Bills
$50 per share, as set out in section 3 of the bill. One of the things that concerned those members who were interrogating the sponsoring senator in the other place was the fact that this oil might be sold in Canada. However, it was made quite clear that the sole purpose was transporting the oil from the United States source in North Dakota to another United States market in Wisconsin and Minnesota. Following up that line of thought, it is also made quite clear in section 5 of the bill that the company, if incorporated, will be subject to the national energy board, which will license the sale of oil by any company anywhere in Canada.
What this company is going to do, therefore, at a cost of $4 million is to build this 10-inch pipe line and, apart from providing jobs in my native province, it will be using the most economic way of transporting their oil by means of an existing pipe line, namely the interprovincial pipe line, and using that common carrier, which will make money for this Canadian company, to transport the oil to markets in Wisconsin and Minnesota. So, Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the standing order, I should like to move that this bill be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines and there hon. members will be able to ask questions on any points that come to mind, section by section.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

the second reading of Bill No. S-21, respecting Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak for a few moments to explain the purpose of this bill to you and to the house. The bill is simply to increase the capitalization of Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company from $5 million to $10 million. Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company was formed in 1917 by an act of this parliament with a capitalization of $10 million. Across the years it became dormant and I believe its assets were transferred to another telephone company in Nova Scotia. In the late twenties, when American Telephone and Telepraph Company and British interests intended to lay a submarine telephone cable across the Atlantic to link up the United States and Canada with Britain, this company, Eastern Telephone and Telegraph, was taken over by American Telephone and Telegraph to hold title to the properties in Canada of the telephone cable system.
A portion of the cable, since it would lie in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia, as well as in

Newfoundland, would belong to Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company. However, it became necessary to shelve the program for the laying of the telephone cable, and since Eastern Telephone and Telegraph was lying dormant there was no need for it to carry the heavy capitalization. In 1929, by act of parliament, the capital of the company was reduced to $75,000.
From 1931 onwards the people in the United States and in Europe who were interested in laying a telephone cable across the Atlantic continued to work to develop a satisfactory cable, and to watch for an opportunity to go ahead with their plans. All during those years the only contact between this continent and Europe by voice was by means of radio, which was always unsatisfactory inasmuch as it depended upon favourable atmospheric conditions and also on the extent of magnetic disturbances.
Then, in the 1950's, discussions were begun again on the matter of laying a telephone cable which would provide a much better link than radio could between this continent and Europe. Finally, in 1953 an agreement was completed between the American Telephone and Telegraph Company, the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation, and Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company, with the postmaster general in the United Kingdom under whose jurisdiction and authority the matter of telecommunication lies in Britain, to build the submarine cable as a joint enterprise.
Under the agreement the cable was to be owned 50 per cent by American Telephone and Telegraph Company, 9 per cent by Canadian Overseas Telecommunications Corporation and 41 per cent by the British postmaster general. The cable was to run for 2,200 miles from Clarenville in Newfoundland to Oban in Scotland and was to be built at a cost of $35 million. Of course, since the contract for construction would require a large expenditure by Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company, it was necessary in 1954 to increase its capitalization so that it could participate in the contract. Therefore in 1954 application was made to this parliament, and the capital of Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company was increasd from $75,000 to $5 million. Chapter 77 of the statutes of 1953-54 authorized the increase in capital.
A cable was thereupon constructed from Sydney Mines in Nova Scotia to Terrence-ville in Newfoundland and thence across New Newfoundland some 60 miles to Clarenville and thence across the Atlantic to Oban in Scotland. This was the first trans-Atlantic telephone cable and the longest submarine cable of its kind in the world. Incidentally,

as a by-product of the laying of this cable to Europe, we enjoyed much better telephone communication with Newfoundland, since the cable gave us better and extra circuits and indeed a substantial saving was made by us in that Canada was not obliged to provide a new cable to Newfoundland.
This present bill asks for further increase because the company now proposes to lay a second cable to Europe. A contract has been entered into between the French republic, and the Federal Republic of Germany in Europe and the American Telephone and Telegraph Company and Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company on this continent to provide a second telephone link, this time with continental Europe, construction of which is now under way. About $3 million has already been spent and I understand that the work in Canada has now been completed. To date the financing has been handled by American Telephone and Telegraph Company by means of a loan to Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company. The purpose of this increase in capitalization is so that shares can be issued to American Telephone and Telegraph Company to take up the amount of its loan to Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company.
The head office of the company is at Halifax in Nova Scotia. These two cables, the one laid in 1954 and the one that is being constructed now, in providing a direct telephone link to Europe increase greatly the facility of communication we have with the European continent. As a joint enterprise between Canada and the United States on one hand, and the United Kingdom, France and Germany on the other, it is an example of what can be accomplished by international cooperation. This cable lying under the ocean for some 2,200 miles could probably never have been laid profitably or economically by any one country. Of the business handled to Europe I understand that about 80 per cent is American and 20 per cent is Canadian.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
As seconder of this bill moved by my colleague the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. MacLellan), I should like to take this opportunity of saying a few words not only because I approve the bill but because of the fact that the North American terminal of this company is located in my home town of Sydney Mines in the constituency of Cape Breton North and Victoria.
To give you a brief background on the history of the company-and I probably may repeat some of what has already been said but I am sure the house will bear with me- may I say that the Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company was incorporated by an
Private Bills
act which was passed in 1917. As indicated in Bill No. S-21, the authorized capital stock at the date of incorporation was $10 million divided into shares of $100 each. In 1929 all of the stock was acquired by American Telephone and Telegraph Company; therefore this company is a wholly owned subsidiary of the American Telephone and Telegraph Company.
At that time it was the intention of the United States company to construct a single panel telephone cable but in 1931 this proposed project was suspended and from then until 1953 Eastern Telephone and Telegraph were inactive.
In 1931 the company's act of incorporation was amended by a special act of parliament whereby the company was authorized to reduce its capital to $75,000 in shares of $100 each. In 1954 a bill was passed in this house to increase the capital to the amount of $5 million, which increase was necessary on account of a contract which had been entered into for the laying of a submarine cable from Clarenville, Newfoundland to Oban, Scotland.
This arrangement consisted of a four-party agreement which brought Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company back into operation. On November 27, 1953 an agreement was effected between Her Majesty's postmaster general in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, American Telephone and Telegraph Company, Canadian Overseas Telecommunications Corporation and Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company. The agreement provided for the construction, at a cost of approximately $35 million, of a cable extending to the points I have mentioned, then to Sydney Mines, Nova Scotia and by radio relay from Sydney Mines to Portland and New York in the United States of America.
This has been a very highly successful venture and consisted originally of 36 circuits, which number was later increased to 48, plus another 24 inter-Canadian circuits from Newfoundland. As I have already mentioned, because of the venture being so successful the circuits have become greatly overloaded, thus necessitating increased facilities.
The new project will add an additional 36 circuits direct to France and I understand that this number will be increased at a later date. The distance covered between Nova Scotia and Scotland is approximately 2,200 miles. The request for this further increase in capital is made necessary because of a contract somewhat similar in nature to the previous one and entered into in 1957 by the French republic, the Federal Republic

Private Bills
of Germany, the American Telephone and Telegraph Company and the Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company. Under this contract there have been constructed or at present there are being constructed telegraph communications and submarine cables from Nova Scotia to Newfoundland and from Newfoundland to Britain.
I understand the amount already spent on this project is approximately $3 million and the cost of materials and equipment used in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia and in Newfoundland amounts to roughly another $1 million.
The head office of this company is located at Halifax, and I might mention that all the employees are Canadians. With reference to the employees, I speak from personal knowledge as to their working conditions, salaries and relations with the company which are of a high calibre. There are 44 employed, with 13 of these positions located in Cape Breton. They are highly skilled technical personnel, a number of whom have been taken directly from the high schools in the Cape Breton area and, because of the excellent training provided by this company in the matter of courses in Montreal and in the United States, plus their natural aptitudes, are extremely well qualified for their positions. I feel that their relations with their employees could be an excellent example for other companies who come from south of the border to pattern themselves after.
The Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company has a board consisting of nine directors. Five of these are Canadians, and included among them is a representative from the Maritime Telephone and Telegraph Company in Nova Scotia and one from the New Brunswick Telephone Company.
It is most appropriate that this company should have selected for their main terminal and highly technical installations the Pond road area in Sydney Mines as their base for the North American continent. Because not too many miles away, still in my constituency of Cape Breton North and Victoria, the great Alexander Graham Bell conducted many of his experiments at Bienn Breagh in Baddeck in the field of communications, and not only in the field of communications but also his many other varied interests, such as the famous hydrofoil H.D.4, and the lighter than air craft, which were numerous, among which of course is the famous Silver Dart.
For the benefit of the C.B.C. I would at this time advise that Alexander Graham Bell was born in Scotland, my own birthplace, and not in Brantford, Ontario, as was stated on the C.B.C. a couple of Sundays ago.

With these few remarks, in closing may I wish the Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company every success in the future, and trust that their operations on Cape Breton Island will continue to grow rapidly.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of pleasure that I join my colleagues, the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. MacLellan) and the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. Muir), in giving my support to Bill No. S-21, respecting Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company. The bill before us requests an authorization for an increase in capital from $5 million to $10 million in order that the second trans-Atlantic telephone cable might be completed. This is the second transAtlantic telephone cable, the first having been completed by the same company in 1956. The work on this cable is already under way and approximately $3 million has been spent to date on its construction, as well as a further $1 million on materials and equipment which were used at Sydney, Nova Scotia and in Newfoundland.
The materials and equipment used in the construction of this trans-Atlantic telephone cable were purchased in the United Kingdom. A good deal of construction work has been carried out in Newfoundland to date, especially with regard to the construction of a tunnel from Clarenville to Terrenceville in that province. I am sure that all hon. members from Newfoundland will be more than happy to support the authorization requested by this company.
In 1954 an act similar to the one presently before us allowed this company to increase its capital stock from the capitalization of $75,000 to its present capital stock of $5 million. As a result of this act they completed the construction of the first trans-Atlantic telephone cable from Oban in Scotland to Clarenville, Newfoundland; thence to Sydney Mines, Nova Scotia, and from there by radio relay to Portland and New York. This turned out to be a very successful venture and this company is to be complimented on its achievement in the field of communications.
There is a long history associated with the laying of submarine cables which dates back to 1851. The first real significant success in this field occurred in 1866 with the laying of a cable from Ireland to Newfoundland. This came about after many failures, and it is a tribute to the engineers of the world that they never lost faith and succeeded in what we today accept as an indispensable convenience and one of strategic importance in time of war. Today we find cables stretching out from Canada across the Atlantic and Pacific to England, Ireland, Bermuda, Australia and New Zealand.

The particular cable that will be constructed it we allow this company to increase its capital stock to $10 million will stretch a distance of approximately 2,200 miles and will provide for the carrying on of 36 conversations at the same time, with a view to having the number of conversations increased, and will eliminate the defects inherent in telephonic communications through radio facilities which are dependent on prevailing atmospheric conditions.
The trans-Atlantic telephone cable which was completed in 1956 is owned by the American Telegraph and Telephone Company, Her Majesty's postmaster general in the United Kingdom and the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation, a crown company of the Canadian government. The breakdown in ownership is: 50 per cent by the American Telegraph and Telephone Company; 41 per cent by the United Kingdom and 9 per cent by the Canadian government.
The trans-Atlantic cable now under construction comes about as the result of an agreement entered into in 1957 by the French republic, the Federal Republic of Germany, the American Telegraph and Telephone Company and the Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company. This cable will stretch from Nova Scotia to Newfoundland and from Newfoundland to the United Kingdom.
As I stated previously, $3 million has already been spent on this project, with a further $1 million spent on materials and equipment. The reason this bill is now before the house is to provide the company with the additional funds that will be necessary to complete the project.
It will be of interest to hon. members to know that this company, although a wholly owned subsidiary of a United States company, has its head office at Halifax in Nova Scotia, that all the employees of the company are Canadians; and I need only refer you to the remarks of my good friend and colleague, the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria, as to the policy the company has adopted in its employment of personnel and of the benefits that have accrued to his constituents as a result of these policies. We as hon. members of this house should not be short in our praise of a company that adopts the attitude this company has in the selection of its personnel. They must, indeed, stand out as an example of the type of company we in Canada are very anxious to attract.
Another point, and a very significant one, is that although this is a wholly owned subsidiary of a United States company, five of this company's directors from a board of directors of nine are Canadians. Often we
Private Bills
note anxieties expressed by individuals in this country over the control of wholly owned subsidiaries. This certainly cannot apply to this company, and it may be that if this attitude were adopted by more companies in a similar position in Canada, many of the present anxieties that find expression would disappear.
It is my opinion, Mr. Speaker, that the operations of this company are of significance; that it has indicated very clearly its ability to carry out ventures of this nature; that the project it has presently undertaken is a very necessary one not only to Canada but to our allies in France and Germany, as well; and that we should support the construction and maintenance of a second transAtlantic telephone cable system by allowing this company to increase its capital stock to $10 million, which will be divided into shares of $100 each.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. E. Bissonnette (Quebec West) moved
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-15, from the Senate, to incorporate the College of General Practice of Canada.
(Translation) :
He said: Mr. Speaker, as a physician member of this house, I am very pleased of the honour being afforded to me of submitting this bill to the approval of the house, in accordance with the expressed wish of my colleagues, the directors of the Medical College of General Practice of Canada an as yet unincorporated medical association which recruits its members among family doctors.
Mr. Speaker, as you may see in section 1 of this bill, a rather impressive number of medical petitioners, from all provinces of Canada, as well as the members of the unincorporated association all of them general practitioners, have asked me to introduce this bill to incorporate them under the name of "The Medical College of General Practice of Canada." I should like to point out that there is an error of translation in the English version, where the word "College" is used instead of "Medical College."
Section 2 indicates that the head office of the association has no permanent character. It is now in Toronto, and it may be located elsewhere, if need be.
Section 3 deserves a bit of attention and a few remarks, since it deals with the very purpose of that college.

Private Bills
According to paragraph a, the purpose of this college is to improve the professional qualifications of its members, and when we speak of professional qualifications, we mean, above all, moral and scientific ones.
The moral qualifications of the medical body, in general, including specialists and general practitioners or family doctors, have always been of a high standard.
In requesting incorporation of their association, the general practitioners therefore seek to sustain and even improve the moral and professional standards of their members, inspiring and urging them to always carry out their mission with a high sense of charity and duty. Their purpose is also to enlighten and direct public opinion in Canada on the importance of their association. They are anxious, moreover, to promote higher scientific standards through post-graduate studies, conferences, medical journals, and publications especially on matters relating to general practice.
To sum up all other paragraphs from b to h of clause 3, I may add that, without disregarding the merits of specialists, this association wishes to attain such scientific standards that the patient will feel even more secure and less inclined to count exclusively, often for minor ailments, on the more expensive care of the specialist.
Representations will be made by the association to schools of medicine in order that medical students who may engage in general practice may follow special courses.
That association was formed under the patronage of the Canadian Medical Association and there is a chapter in each province. The bill does not ask for any legislative powers with regard to the medical profession, nor in respect of teaching and discipline. Indeed, the association does not wish to encroach upon the authority of provincial medical colleges. It only asks for general administrative powers for internal control.
Thus, in section 9, the bill provides among other general powers, the right to acquire, possess, dispose of or mortgage chattels and real estate, to collect contributions from its members for the purpose of setting up an administrative fund, to borrow, negotiate, invest its funds, and participate in charitable activities. In brief, the association asks for all ordinary privileges enjoyed by every well-run corporation of the same type.
(Text):

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words as seconder

of this bill. We in the medical profession have a responsibility to provide to the people of Canada medical care at the highest level at a reasonable cost. The best way this can be done is through the well-educated, well-trained and properly informed general practitioner. This has been the driving force behind the creation of the College of General Practice and I am sure indicates to the country as a whole that the medical profession has accepted that responsibility.
Recently a survey by a medical economist has revealed the rule that the proportion of the gross national product of a nation devoted to medical care tends to remain constant. This seems not to have too much relationship to whether or not the schemes are socialistic or otherwise.
As my colleague the hon. member from Quebec West (Mr. Bissonnette) has pointed out, the objectives of this association are clearly set out in clause 3 of the bill. They have as their prime objective improving the professional qualifications of the members of the college of general practice. Subclause a is a general subclause which covers all qualifications. Certainly subclause c is an important one, its purpose being to help enlighten and direct public opinion in Canada in relation to general practice. Subclauses d, e and f provide for more extensive information and teaching of the general practitioner in a post-graduate manner.
As I said, this bill relates to the general practitioner and is an indication that the medical profession is assuming in a free society its responsibility to promote the aims and objectives of the profession in which its members are engaged, I commend it to the house for its study.

Mr. Speaker, not being a member of that profession of which the two previous speakers are distinguished members it may be presumptuous on my part to speak to the bill before us.
One objective of the college is to enlighten public opinion in Canada in relation to the general practice of medicine. I know that in the past when suggestions have been made for what we could call state medicine, socialized medicine, national health insurance, or something of that nature, there have been objections from members of the medical profession-I will not say from the profession in its entirety-objections to the idea of public health or public hospital insurance coverage, and things of that nature. I hope that one of the things this college will not engage itself

in after it is established, in its efforts to enlighten and direct public opinion, is an antihealth plans approach, as some members of the medical profession have done in years gone by. I do not say this of the majority, but I hope this college will not do this, and I am sure it will not, because public opinion generally and opinion amongst the medical profession have altered toward the question of government-sponsored health and hospital insurance plans.
Another thing to which it might direct its energies in its enlightenment and direction of public opinion-and incidentally, I might say this as an aside, the phrase "direct public opinion" is a bit strong, but nevertheless it is there-to a greater degree is an explanation to the general public of the use to which pharmaceuticals, especially the newer ones on the market, can be put, bringing to the attention of the general public more so than it has in the past some of the detrimental effects which can arise from the indiscriminate use of those newer so-called antibiotics, in so far as the individual and society are concerned. There certainly appears to be a great deal of the witch doctor type of mumbo-jumbo involved in the development of pharmaceuticals and in the nomenclature surrounding them, and also surrounding what they are designed to do. I think this college, along with the provincial colleges of physicians and surgeons, could do a great service to society by going more fully into the field of the pharmaceuticals manufactured by the drug companies and what they mean to the individual and how they can be helpful or, in some cases, injurious to the individual himself.
Another thing which I would like very much to see this college consider doing and engage itself in-probably as an unincorporated society it is doing it now; I think they could expand a great deal in that regard -is to encourage, support, promote or engage itself in research concerning cancer. This is one field in which cancer research foundations and other organizations, universities, and so forth, have been engaged in for many years, and it is one of the important physical ailments for which an answer has not been found. I should like to see some of the large drug manufacturing concerns here and in the United States engage themselves in cancer research. Unfortunately, they do not do so, or if they do it is only to an extremely limited degree by grants to foundations or to universities. Here I believe the college on a national basis or national level could do a great deal toward promoting, encouraging and fostering research in cancer and in ways and means to overcome it.
Private Bills
There is one thing that perhaps the hon. member who sponsored the bill could clear up when he closes the debate. I am sure we would all like to see this bill receive second reading this evening. I wonder whether he would indicate to the house the relationship that there will be between this college and the various provincial colleges of physicians and surgeons which exist because I note that one of the objects of the college is to promote high standards in the general practice of medicine in the provinces through the medium of provincial chapters of the college. I wonder whether it is the intention to establish provincial chapters of this college or whether, for instance, the present British Columbia college of physicians and surgeons is already a part of the unincorporated college which exists at the moment.
In the few moments that are left could the hon. member explain to the house what is the relationship at the moment and what will be the relationship between those colleges when the bill is passed?

In answering the questions of the hon. member who has just resumed his seat, I should say that I have given precisely those explanations when introducing the bill; I said that the college has no legislative powers and does not ask for such powers. Consequently, it may not exercise any authority with regard to medical colleges in the other provinces, which have been conferred legislative as well as administrative powers. The college only wants administrative authority in respect of internal control, in order to operate efficiently. It has no authority whatsoever with regard to education, nor the discipline of its members from a legal point of view. Therefore, if you will read the bill closely, you will see that there it asks for nothing but administrative powers. There is no question of legislative powers.

Business of the House (Translation):

Those provincial chapters mean that there will be a special administrative council for each province, but its character will be purely administrative, to the exclusion of any legislative authority in respect of medical teaching or the discipline of physicians coming under the various provincial medical colleges. But, in each province, there will be a chapter subordinate to the central association, which now has its head office in Toronto.
